payload.title: Size the server's sequence→bytes ring from the grant budget (fixed 65536 entries can be outrun)
payload.body: From iss-fbzcsr1. The server keeps a fixed 65536-entry ring mapping sequence numbers to (rpc, offset, len) so it can answer RESEND_SEQ. With a 16 MiB budget and small payloads, a session could in principle outrun it; evicted entries are skipped (counted as misses) and those losses fall back to the stall timer, which is correct but slow. Size the ring from the negotiated budget and payload size, or evict by age rather than count, and add a test that forces eviction and checks recovery still completes. Also untested: the fallback to plain DATA past 2^32 sequence numbers (~5 TB in one session).

patch.title: Bound the server's sequence→bytes table by age first, with a budget-derived size cap (today: a fixed 65536 entries)
patch.body:
From iss-fbzcsr1. To answer RESEND_SEQ, the sender keeps a ring mapping each sequence number to (rpc, offset, len). It is a fixed 65536 entries, which is both too big and too small: ~4× more than needed at 1183-byte payloads, and outrun at ~100-byte payloads with a large budget (16 MiB ÷ 100 B ≈ 168k in flight). An evicted entry is skipped and counted as a miss, and that loss falls back to the stall timer, so recovery is still correct but slow: a quiet performance cliff, not a bug.

Use both rules, which are complementary, not alternatives:
1. **Age is the primary rule.** Keep an entry only while a loss report for it could still arrive: a few RTTs (start with 3 × srtt, floored for tiny RTTs, and account for the client's RESEND_SEQ repeats, which are two repair delays apart, dec-cjth7tv). This is self-tuning and independent of payload size.
2. **A size cap bounds memory.** entries ≤ 2 × budget ÷ current payload size, recomputed as the budget moves (dec-550khn9), plus an absolute ceiling (e.g. 256k entries ≈ 4 MB) so one session can't run away. The cap normally never engages: it covers a stalled client that stops reporting, a huge budget with tiny payloads, and a deliberately abusive peer. That last case matters once the demo is public (iss-fzz5beq), since this is memory a remote client can make the server allocate.

Consider shrinking each entry too (a per-session rpc index instead of the 8-byte RPCID takes it from ~16 to ~8 bytes).

Acceptance:
- A test forces eviction (small payloads, a large budget, or a paused client) and checks every fixture still arrives intact, with the miss counter showing the fallback was exercised.
- A test shows memory stays bounded under the cap with a stalled client.
- At 1% × 50 ms through the proxy, recovery timing is unchanged from today (no regression from the smaller working set).
- Per-session memory at a 16 MiB budget is reported.

Also untested: the fallback to plain DATA past 2^32 sequence numbers (~5 TB in one session).

payload.title: G10 — Apps steer bytes in flight: a page controls what arrives next, and stops paying for bytes it never needed
payload.body:
Requested by the user on 2026-09-22 after asking whether receiver-driven grants let an app tune delivery to its own needs. No browser API today lets a page throttle or repoint a response that is already in flight; HTTP/3 priority is a hint to the server, and cancelling loses the bytes already received. HTTP4's grants are byte ceilings the receiver issues continuously, so the page decides what arrives next, every round trip.

Primary metric: in the viewport demo, the % of delivered subresource bytes the user never needed (images scrolled past or abandoned before being seen). Target ≤ 10%, lower is better. A baseline over plain HTTP/3 on the same page is reported alongside it, where the figure is expected to be much higher, because bytes already requested keep coming.

Secondary, reported not targeted: how long a change of priority takes to show up in what arrives (aim ≤ 2 RTT), and that pausing and resuming a transfer costs no re-fetched bytes.

payload.title: Application-steered delivery: expose HTTP4's byte-level control to pages (G10)
payload.body:
Parent for G10 (gol-mg557kh). The scheduler already decides byte ceilings every round trip, GRANT already carries an unused priority byte, and the Service Worker already knows each request's destination. What's missing is an API for pages, a server that honours the priority, the pause/resume/cancel and partial-fetch verbs, sensible automatic defaults, and a demo that shows something HTTP/3 cannot do.

Limits to keep in mind throughout: QUIC's congestion control still sets the total rate, so this allocates the pie rather than enlarging it; a change of priority takes about one round trip to show up; and more control means more ways to starve a transfer, which is G6's concern (Phase 3 aging).

payload.title: Priority and deadline API: let a page classify requests, and schedule by weight or deadline instead of strict SRPT
payload.body:
For G10. The public API grows a per-request class, e.g. `handle.fetch(url, { http4: { class: "critical" | "normal" | "background", deadline?: number } })`, plus a way to change a live transfer's class (see the pause/resume issue).

Scheduler (client/src/scheduler.ts): today it is strict shortest-remaining-first, with invariants tested by simulation. Add a policy layer:
- **Weighted classes:** critical takes budget ahead of normal, which takes it ahead of background, with SRPT inside each class. Background is not starved outright, because G6 aging still applies.
- **Deadlines:** when a request carries one, order by earliest deadline first among those that can still make it; fall back to SRPT.
- Keep the existing invariants (budget never exceeded, grants only rise) and extend the randomized simulation to cover classes and deadlines.

The class also goes out in GRANT's priority byte (0 = most urgent) for the server issue.

Acceptance: unit tests show a critical request issued during a large background transfer takes the budget within one grant cycle; the simulation finds no invariant violations with mixed classes; the existing SRPT-only behaviour is unchanged when no class is given.

payload.title: Server honours GRANT's priority byte when choosing which RPC to send next
payload.body:
For G10. The sender orders work by its own shortest-remaining rule across RPCs (dec for the passive sender), and ignores the priority byte the client already sends in every GRANT. That usually agrees with the client, but not when the page has said otherwise: a large critical asset should beat a small background one.

Change the send-loop choice to: control packets, then META, then packet 0, then resends, then new data, and within each kind order by (priority, then remaining bytes). Keep the G2 check and the grant ceilings exactly as they are; this only reorders what is already allowed.

Acceptance: a sender unit test with a fake transport shows a high-priority large RPC served before a low-priority small one, and no change when all priorities are equal (the existing tests must pass untouched). The server's own metric for reordering is optional.

payload.title: Pause, resume and cancel a transfer in flight (pause and resume cost no re-fetched bytes)
payload.body:
For G10, and the capability HTTP/3 can't offer in a browser.
- **Pause:** stop granting. The transfer freezes with no protocol change at all; the server simply has nothing to send.
- **Resume:** grant again and it continues from the same offset. Nothing already received is re-fetched.
- **Cancel:** the client must be able to release the transfer and the server its state. Options: a new CANCEL packet (additive, wire v2 style, negotiated or simply ignored by older servers), or rely on the server's idle eviction (dec-yk031c3's default 60 s) with the client just forgetting the RPC. Weigh the cost: without CANCEL, a cancelled RPC holds server memory (including its sequence-table entries, iss-e0n6q55) until it times out.
- The API: `transfer.pause()`, `.resume()`, `.cancel()`, or an AbortSignal that maps to cancel. Note that today aborting rejects the caller but the transfer keeps running (dec-xkak0cd).

Acceptance: a browser test pauses a large transfer mid-flight, shows bytes stop arriving within about one RTT, resumes it and shows 0 duplicate bytes and a correct SHA-256. Cancel frees the server's RPC state promptly (assert via metrics).

payload.title: Partial fetches over HTTP4: serve Range requests natively instead of falling back to plain HTTP
payload.body:
For G10. Grants are byte offsets, so a partial fetch is the protocol's natural shape, yet the library sends every Range request to the platform fetch (dec-xkak0cd) because there was no way to express it. Add:
- **Library:** honour a Range request by granting only that window and resolving a 206 Response with Content-Range, plus a direct API, e.g. `handle.fetch(url, { http4: { range: [start, end] } })`.
- **Client internals:** a transfer that completes at a byte range rather than at total_size, without marking the rest lost.
- **META:** Content-Length semantics for a partial response; decide whether the server must send anything new (probably not: total_size is already in every DATA).
- Uses: a low-quality image preview from the first N KB of a progressive JPEG, the first seconds of a media file, or resuming an interrupted download from an offset.

Acceptance: a browser test fetches [0, 20 KiB) of a large fixture, checks the bytes against the manifest's prefix, and shows the server sent nothing beyond the grant (G2 = 0); a second fetch of the remainder completes the file with 0 duplicate bytes.

payload.title: Automatic priority classes in the Service Worker from each request's destination
payload.body:
For G10. The worker already knows each request's `destination` (style, script, font, image, fetch) and forwards it to the page (dec-5kzdkfq). Map it to a default class so a site gets sensible behaviour with no code: style, script and font critical; fetch/XHR normal; images background, or normal above the fold. Sites can override per request through the API (iss-j9tm9w8) or with a small config passed to install().

Check whether a request's own priority is visible to the worker (fetchpriority / Request.priority in Chrome 153) and use it when present; document what is and isn't exposed.

Acceptance: on the demo site with no site-side changes, the stylesheet, script and font complete before the images in a measured load, and the transport report shows the classes that were applied.

payload.title: Viewport-driven demo: images are granted only while visible, measuring G10's wasted bytes vs HTTP/3
payload.body:
The showcase for G10 (gol-mg557kh), and the thing HTTP/3 can't do in a browser. Extend examples/demo-site (or add a second page) with a long gallery of large images where an IntersectionObserver drives delivery:
- An image entering the viewport, or getting close, is granted aggressively.
- One scrolled away is paused (no further grants), keeping the bytes already received.
- Coming back resumes where it stopped, with no re-fetch.
- The panel shows live grants per image, so pausing and resuming are visible.

Measurement: scripted scroll (headless) that visits part of the gallery and abandons the rest. Report the % of delivered subresource bytes never needed, over HTTP4 and, as a baseline, over plain HTTP/3 with the same script and images (where requested bytes keep arriving). That ratio is G10's measurement.

Depends on the priority API (iss-j9tm9w8) and pause/resume (iss-vg5kzjf).

Acceptance: a headless test prints both percentages and records the HTTP4 one as a G10 measurement; the page works (loading everything eagerly) when HTTP4 is off.

payload.title: Compress text assets over HTTP4: today CSS and JS travel raw while HTTP/3 sends them gzipped or brotlied
payload.body:
HTTP4 deliberately carries raw bytes (dec-vy1ddyw dropped the proposal's extra encryption layer, and dec-pa5xv8m left content-encoding out of META on purpose). That's fine for images and fonts, which are already compressed, but a text-heavy site sends 3–4× more bytes than HTTP/3 does. Any public comparison (the demo, G3, G9) would show it, and the cause would look like the protocol rather than a missing feature.

Design points:
- **Negotiation:** add a capability bit to HELLO (dec-cjth7tv) for the encodings the client can decode, and allow `content-encoding` in META as an allowlisted field (a wire change; update docs, vectors and both codecs). Without the capability the server keeps sending raw bytes, so old clients are unaffected.
- **Decoding, the practical catch:** a Response constructed in JavaScript is NOT auto-decoded by the browser, so the client must decompress itself. `DecompressionStream` covers gzip and deflate natively; **brotli is not available** in Chrome's DecompressionStream, so brotli would need a WASM decoder (weigh ~200 KB of library against the extra ~15% over gzip). Start with gzip.
- **Server:** prefer a pre-compressed sibling (`style.css.gz`) so nothing is compressed per request; fall back to compressing on the fly with a size threshold, or to raw. `http4d serve` should pick this up automatically.
- **Accounting:** total_size and the sequence numbering describe the compressed stream; the ETag and the integrity suite's SHA-256 must keep describing the decompressed bytes, or the fixtures and manifests need a clear rule. Get this right first: it touches G1's checks.
- **Interaction:** chunk dedupe (the spike issue) compresses badly across chunk boundaries; measure compression alone before combining them.

Acceptance: with gzip negotiated, text fixtures transfer at roughly their gzip size, decompress to bytes matching the manifest, G1 and G2 are unaffected, and a browser test compares transferred bytes for a text-heavy page against plain HTTP/3. Without the capability, or with the server flag off, behaviour is byte-identical to today.

payload.title: Spike: measure what content-addressed chunk reuse would actually save, before building any of it
payload.body:
Idea (from the user, 2026-09-22): keep a content-addressed store of chunks on both sides, so a client only fetches the parts of a resource it doesn't already have. HTTP4 suits the delivery half unusually well: because the receiver grants byte ranges, a client that knows it already holds bytes [0, 40 KiB) simply doesn't grant them, and the passive server sends nothing. No new verb is needed for the transfer itself.

The hard parts are the usual ones, so **measure before building**:
- **Content-defined chunking:** fixed blocks break when a byte is inserted; boundaries must come from a rolling hash (rsync, FastCDC).
- **A manifest:** the client needs the new resource's chunk hashes before it can decide what to grant, which costs a round trip or a push with packet 0 (zsync's model). Small resources can't pay for it.
- **A client chunk store** (IndexedDB or the Cache API) with eviction, plus verification that the assembled bytes match the resource's hash.
- **Cross-origin sharing is out:** browsers partitioned caches because a shared content-addressed cache lets a site probe what a user has. Savings are therefore within one origin: version-to-version deltas and repetition inside a site.

Spike (no protocol changes, offline analysis):
1. Take realistic before/after pairs: a JS bundle across a few releases, a CSS file, and a set of site images.
2. Compute the reuse content-defined chunking would give (try 4/8/16 KiB average chunks), as bytes that need no transfer.
3. Compare against: gzip/brotli alone (the compression issue), and a server-side delta (RFC 3229 style, which needs no chunk store but does need old versions kept).
4. Report bytes saved, the manifest's own cost, and the CPU cost of hashing.

Decide from the numbers: build it, do delta encoding instead, or drop it. Record the result as a finding either way.

payload.body:
`npm run matrix` on main 69a27c6 (wire v2 with session-wide loss detection; hang-guard deadlines per dec-smr579z). Full pool, 11 fixtures, 61.1 MiB, 2,629 s total.

**Passing (5):** 0×0, 0×50, 0×150, 1×0, 5×0. All 22/22 intact.

**Failing (4):** 1×50, 1×150, 5×50, 5×150, each 21/22 (G1 95.5%). G2 = 0 in all nine cells.

The failure is the same everywhere, and is NOT a deadline (the guards, 23–148 min, were never reached) and NOT corruption:

The largest fixture fails in the concurrent pass after receiving only ~18–38 KB, while the same fixture completes in the single pass of the same cell. Strict SRPT leaves it starved of grants while the other ten transfers run; it holds a small unrepaired hole from its initial grant, exhausts the client's 10-attempt recovery limit, and the fetch is failed. See the finding and issue for diagnosis.

payload.title: A transfer starved by SRPT can be abandoned by its own client: under loss, the 50 MiB fixture fails after 10 recovery attempts while holding ~30 KB, in every lossy cell with RTT ≥ 50 ms
payload.body:
Official matrix run (mea for the G5 run), 2026-09-22, main 69a27c6. Identical in cells 1×50, 1×150, 5×50 and 5×150, and only in the concurrent pass:

    50m.bin: no progress after 10 recovery attempts (17685–37728 / 52428800 bytes)

The same fixture completes in the single pass of the same cell, so neither the path nor the file is at fault. In the concurrent pass, strict SRPT (dec for the scheduler) gives the largest transfer no budget until the other ten finish. It sits at roughly its 4 KiB initial grant with a small hole that never gets repaired, each attempt counts against ClientOptions.maxRecoveries (10), and the fetch is failed even though the session is healthy and every other transfer is progressing.

Two contributing mechanisms, to be told apart by instrumenting a reproduction:
1. **Recovery accounting:** a starved transfer's attempts should probably not count as failures at all; "no progress" is expected when nothing is granted. The waiting check in transport.tick() only skips the stall path when received >= granted, which is false while a hole is outstanding.
2. **The server's sequence table (iss-e0n6q55):** the concurrent pass moves >50,000 packets for the other transfers, past the fixed 65,536-entry ring, so the starved transfer's entries are evicted and its RESEND_SEQ finds nothing to resend. That is the predicted cliff, now with a failing case.

This is also G6's territory (gol-d4jyb3j, starvation), showing up as a correctness failure rather than slow completion.

payload.title: BUG: a starved transfer is abandoned after 10 recovery attempts, failing the fetch on a healthy session (blocks G5 = 100%)
payload.body:
From the official matrix run (mea-dm4yv3e, fnd-g4d7cqm). In every lossy cell with RTT ≥ 50 ms, the concurrent pass fails 50m.bin with "no progress after 10 recovery attempts" while it holds only ~18–38 KB of 50 MiB. The same fixture completes when fetched alone. G2 stays 0 and nothing is corrupted: the client simply gives up on a transfer the scheduler has starved.

Diagnosis first, with a reproduction (one cell, e.g. `npm run matrix -- --cells 1x50`, or a focused browser test with the pool fetched concurrently at 1% × 50 ms), instrumented to show, for the starved transfer: granted vs received, the outstanding hole, each recovery attempt and what it sent (REQ / GRANT / RESEND / RESEND_SEQ), and whether the server found the sequence entries (its miss counter).

Two mechanisms to separate, both plausibly at play:
1. **Recovery accounting.** "No progress" is expected while nothing is granted, so those attempts shouldn't count toward maxRecoveries. transport.tick() only skips the stall path when received >= granted, which is false while a hole is outstanding. Candidate fix: count an attempt as failed only when the transfer has outstanding grant *and* the session is otherwise idle; or don't fail a transfer at all while the session is making progress elsewhere, relying on the caller's own timeout.
2. **Server sequence-table eviction (iss-e0n6q55).** The concurrent pass pushes >50,000 packets for the other transfers past the fixed 65,536-entry ring, so the starved transfer's entries are gone and its RESEND_SEQ finds nothing. Fixing that issue (age-based retention plus a budget-derived cap) may resolve this on its own.

Also consider whether SRPT should reserve a trickle for a starved transfer (that is G6/Phase 3 aging, gol-d4jyb3j) — but this bug must be fixed regardless, because a starved transfer should wait, not fail.

Acceptance: `npm run matrix` reaches G5 = 100% on the full pool, with no fetch failing for lack of progress while the session is healthy, and a regression test that fetches the pool concurrently at 1% × 50 ms and asserts every fixture completes.

patch.body:
Rescoped by dec-smr579z (answers que-8yddjxq). G5 now scores correctness: the matrix deadline is a hang guard (tests/support/suite.ts cellDeadlineMs), with a 3 h total cap. Speed under loss moved to G9 (gol-1ga4ayw).

payload.title: Deployment TLS: three cert modes (dev / file / acme) with Trusted() driving HTTPS pages and hash advertisement; ACME answers HTTP-01 and TLS-ALPN-01; -origin allowlist; -metrics local by default
payload.body:
Implemented in iss-fzz5beq.
- **Modes:** `-cert dev` (unchanged default, in-memory cert + hash pinning), `-cert file:<cert.pem>,<key.pem>` (re-read on SIGHUP through GetCertificate over an atomic.Pointer; a failed reload keeps the old pair), `-cert acme` (autocert, `-domain` repeatable, `-acme-email`, `-acme-cache` required so restarts don't re-ask the CA, `-acme-staging` to rehearse).
- **Trusted() drives the rest:** with a real certificate the TCP listener serves HTTPS via ServeTLS (so Go sets up HTTP/2), HTTPURL becomes https://, config.json omits certHash and spkiHash, and the loopback origin rule follows the server's own scheme.
- **Client:** an empty certHash is treated as absent, so the browser validates the chain normally rather than pinning "".
- **Redirect listener:** `-redirect <addr>` serves only 301s and the ACME HTTP-01 path; default :80 in acme mode, off otherwise, refused with -cert dev.
- **ACME challenges:** HTTP-01 on the redirect listener and TLS-ALPN-01 free on the HTTPS listener (acme-tls/1 in NextProtos), so either alone suffices.
- **Origins:** `-origin scheme://host[:port]`, repeatable, validated at startup with default ports normalised; the same check gates the h3 CORS and Timing-Allow-Origin headers.
- **Metrics:** `-metrics off|local|public`, default local in serve mode (non-loopback gets 404, not 403), public for the sandbox so existing tests are unaffected.

payload.title: Strict SRPT inverts the right order for client-rendered (React-style) sites: it finishes the small stylesheet and fonts before the large JS bundle that the page actually needs to render
payload.body:
Raised by the user on 2026-09-22. The client schedules strictly shortest-remaining-first (dec for the SRPT scheduler). On a client-rendered site the JS bundle is the largest asset and the stylesheet is small, so SRPT deliberately delivers CSS and fonts first, while nothing meaningful can paint until the bundle has downloaded, compiled and run. Chrome's own priorities do something similar for a different reason (render-blocking CSS is highest priority, and a page can only nudge it with fetchpriority; HTTP/3 priorities are hints).

So HTTP4's default policy is currently worse than neutral for this common architecture, and the fix is expressible here in a way it isn't over HTTP/3: a page can grant the bundle everything until it is in, then release CSS and fonts (iss-j9tm9w8 priority classes, iss-p891483 automatic classes). That argues for a "client-rendered" profile that inverts the defaults.

Confounder to settle before claiming a win: Chrome compiles JavaScript while it downloads (streaming compilation) and parses CSS incrementally, but the client library resolves a Response only once the whole body has arrived, so HTTP4 currently forfeits that overlap. Ordering the bundle first could be cancelled out by starting compilation later. See the streaming-body issue.

payload.title: Stream response bodies so the browser can parse and compile while bytes arrive (today a Response resolves only when the transfer completes)
payload.body:
From the client-rendering discussion (see the SRPT-inversion finding). The client library builds a Response from a complete ArrayBuffer (dec-xkak0cd), so the browser sees nothing until the last byte. Chrome streams JavaScript compilation and parses CSS incrementally as bytes arrive over HTTP/3, so HTTP4 currently gives that overlap up on exactly the largest, most critical assets. On a big bundle that can cost more than any scheduling win.

Build:
- **Client:** resolve the Response as soon as META arrives, with a ReadableStream body fed by the contiguous prefix of the reassembly buffer as it grows (the prefix is already tracked). Out-of-order bytes wait until the gap fills, which is what a stream requires.
- **Backpressure:** a slow reader should throttle grants, which is exactly what the receiver-driven design can express; don't buffer without bound.
- **Errors mid-stream:** a transfer that fails after the Response resolved must error the stream, not silently truncate. Make sure a truncated body can never be mistaken for a complete one (that would undermine G1's guarantees at the library level).
- **Service Worker path:** a streamed body must survive being forwarded from the page to the worker (today the body is transferred as one ArrayBuffer, dec-5kzdkfq); check whether a ReadableStream can be transferred, or chunk it over the MessageChannel.
- Keep a non-streaming path for callers that want bytes (the demo and tests use it).

Acceptance: a browser test shows a large module script beginning to compile before its transfer completes (e.g. via Resource/Element timing or an in-page marker), the SHA-256 of a streamed body matches, a mid-stream failure errors the stream, and a slow reader visibly slows grants rather than growing memory.

patch.title: Whether SRPT helps or hurts a client-rendered site depends on its bundling shape: it is wrong for one big bundle, and right for code-split apps where Chrome's CSS-first priorities are the problem
patch.body:
Raised by the user on 2026-09-22, and corrected by them the same day with what they see in practice.

**Shape A, bundled:** one large JS bundle, one small stylesheet. Strict SRPT (dec for the scheduler) finishes the CSS and fonts first, while nothing paints until the bundle has downloaded, compiled and run. Here our default is the wrong order.

**Shape B, code-split (the user's experience, and common):** 5–6 stylesheets of 64 KB+ each, plus many small JS chunks of 2–10 KB that are all blocked. Here SRPT is the *right* order: every small chunk finishes ahead of the large stylesheets. Chrome does the opposite, because render-blocking CSS gets its highest priority and a page can only nudge that with fetchpriority, so the chunks queue behind the CSS. This is a case where HTTP4's default already beats the browser's scheduling, and it should be measurable.

Consequences:
- The default policy can't be right for both shapes, so this needs a per-site profile (iss-j9tm9w8, iss-p891483) rather than one global rule.
- Shape B suits HTTP4 well for another reason: the 4 KiB initial grant (dec-550khn9) covers a 2–10 KB chunk in about one round trip, with no grant exchange.
- **What transport can't fix:** code splitting's dependency waterfalls, where a chunk is only discovered after its parent parses. That needs preloading or a manifest; claiming a transport win there would be wrong.
- Shape A's confounder still stands: the library resolves a Response only when the whole body has arrived, so HTTP4 forfeits Chrome's streaming compilation (iss-x6ess8x). That matters most for the large assets in both shapes: the bundle in A, the 64 KB stylesheets in B.

payload.title: Benchmark real app shapes: code-split (many 2–10 KB chunks + 64 KB stylesheets) and bundled, HTTP4 vs HTTP/3, to time-to-interactive
payload.body:
From the client-rendering discussion (fnd-ysspr7x). The interesting metric for a client-rendered app is not first paint but time to interactive: every critical chunk downloaded, compiled, run and the app mounted.

Two page shapes, both generated so they're reproducible:
- **Code-split (the user's real-world shape):** 5–6 stylesheets of 64 KB+, plus 40–60 JS chunks of 2–10 KB, including a second-level chunk or two discovered only after a parent parses (the waterfall).
- **Bundled:** one 400 KB–1 MB JS bundle plus one small stylesheet.

Stacks per shape: HTTP/3 with Chrome's own priorities; HTTP/3 with fetchpriority hints on the chunks; HTTP4 with today's SRPT default; HTTP4 with a JS-first profile (once iss-j9tm9w8 lands). Report with and without streaming bodies (iss-x6ess8x) once that exists, since it may dominate on the large assets.

Conditions: clean loopback, plus 50 ms and 150 ms RTT through the impairment proxy, and one lossy cell.

Expected, to be confirmed or refuted: on the code-split shape HTTP4's SRPT should beat Chrome's CSS-first ordering, because the chunks finish first; on the bundled shape today's default should lose until a profile inverts it. Acceptance: `npm run bench:app` prints per-shape, per-stack time-to-interactive (plus first paint and per-asset completion order), and the result is recorded as a finding. No workload tuning to make HTTP4 win.

| Condition | HTTP4 p50/p90/p99/p99.9 | best h3 p50/p90/p99/p99.9 | G3 |

| clean loopback | 0.7 / 1.5 / 13.3 / 41.0 | 1.7 / 3.3 / 13.1 / 46.3 | −1.5% |

payload.title: Cause of the loss-case regression: small replies queue behind bulk datagrams in quic-go's 32-datagram sender queue, so receiver priority doesn't survive to the wire (+95 ms from ONE background transfer at 1%×50 ms)
payload.body:
Isolated in the G3 work, 1% × 50 ms, HTTP4 p50 for small replies by background load:

| Background | HTTP4 p50 | h3 p50 |
|---|---|---|
| none | 52.0 ms (≈1 RTT) | 54.2 ms |
| 1 download | 146.6 ms (+95) | 86.6 ms (+32) |
| 4 downloads | 142.6 ms | 114.2 ms |

Alone, HTTP4 is ideal. A single competing bulk transfer costs ~95 ms, which matches quic-go's 32-datagram send queue (~38 KB) draining at the ~0.3 MB/s the lossy link allows (~125 ms). SRPT decides what to *enqueue*, but bulk datagrams already sitting in the sender's FIFO block a newly granted small reply.

The same model explains the other conditions: at 0% × 150 ms the queue drains in ~3 ms and HTTP4 wins by 28%; on loopback it is ~1–3 ms and HTTP4 wins on p50/p90. So this is an implementation limit of the sender, not of receiver-driven grants, and it is the highest-value fix for G3.

payload.title: Measurement bias, now fixed: the bench page stopped HTTP/3's clock after a Resource Timing lookup that polls on a 5 ms timer, inflating every earlier h3-vs-HTTP4 comparison in HTTP4's favour
payload.body:
Found while building the G3 benchmark (iss-3ecq28b). client/bench's `one()` recorded a request's completion *after* awaiting the nextHopProtocol lookup, which only happens for h3 and polls on a 5 ms timer. h3 times were therefore padded by up to ~5 ms per request, while HTTP4's were not. Fixed: the clock now stops on the body, and the protocol check is tallied once per window, never inside a timed request.

Affected, and to be re-measured before being quoted:
- fnd-bcd98yb (BDP budget: HTTP4 vs h3 on 50 MiB and the 8-asset batch)
- fnd-6k60b8k (session-wide loss detection: batch ratios 0.89–1.14×)
- fnd-e667gya (already superseded by fnd-6k60b8k)

The bias is small in absolute terms (≤5 ms per request), so it matters most where HTTP4's margin was thin: the batch ratios near 1.0×, not the 50 MiB bulk numbers measured in seconds. G9's benchmark (iss-7kq1d97) should use the corrected harness.

payload.title: Keep the sender's datagram queue shallow so receiver priority survives to the wire (the main G3 fix: +95 ms from one bulk transfer)
payload.body:
From the G3 benchmark (fnd-pp7zab7). SRPT chooses what the sender *enqueues*, but quic-go's send queue holds up to 32 datagrams (~38 KB) in FIFO order. On a slow path that queue takes ~125 ms to drain, so a newly granted small reply waits behind bulk datagrams already queued. Measured: one competing background transfer adds ~95 ms to HTTP4's p50 at 1% × 50 ms, which is the whole of the −33.5% G3 regression there.

Options, cheapest first:
1. **Self-clocking:** the sender keeps at most k datagrams (k small, e.g. 2–4) outstanding in quic-go's queue, and only enqueues the next when one is sent. quic-go's SendDatagram blocks when the queue is full, so the send loop can measure and throttle itself. This costs a little throughput headroom.
2. **Re-pick after every datagram:** the send loop already re-picks work each iteration; with a shallow queue that re-pick actually matters, so combine it with 1.
3. **Priority-aware enqueue:** if quic-go ever exposes it, place urgent datagrams ahead of queued bulk. Not available today.

Measure: `npm run bench:g3 --conditions 1x50` before and after, plus the clean and 0×150 conditions to confirm no loss of throughput; and the background-isolation table from fnd-pp7zab7 (0, 1 and 4 background transfers).

Acceptance: at 1% × 50 ms, HTTP4's small-reply p50 with 1 background transfer is within ~20 ms of its no-background p50 (52 ms), and G3 at that condition is no longer negative. Bulk throughput on a clean path drops by no more than ~10%.

Re-run and re-record, with the corrected harness:
- fnd-bcd98yb: the 8-asset batch and api.json ratios at 0/50/150 ms (the 50 MiB figures, in seconds, are effectively unaffected).

- Supersede both findings with corrected numbers rather than editing them, so the record shows what was believed when.

This also feeds G9's benchmark (iss-7kq1d97), which must use the corrected harness from the start.

payload.title: G3's target is ≥80% lower p99 than HTTP/3. The first measurement says −33% to +28%. Keep the target, revise it, or judge the proposal's claim refuted?
payload.body:
From mea-fxsg6j2 and fnd-xj391f2. Measured G3: clean −1.5% (noise), 1%×50 ms −33.5%, 0%×150 ms +28.4%. Two things are now clearer than when the target was set:
- **80% was probably never reachable.** A small reply over a modern h3 stack already completes in roughly one round trip under load, and HTTP4 cannot be 80% below one round trip. The proposal's figure appears to assume an HTTP/3 baseline that queues small responses far worse than Chrome + quic-go actually do.
- **There is a real, fixable regression** (fnd-pp7zab7, iss-dy53a59): bulk datagrams sitting in the sender's queue delay small replies by ~95 ms on a lossy path. Fixing that should recover the 1%×50 ms condition, but nothing suggests it would approach +80%.

options.option: Revise the target to 'never worse, and ≥20% better where latency dominates' (recommended)
options.consequence: Honest and still meaningful: it asks HTTP4 to beat h3 on the case it is designed for (high RTT, small replies under load, where it already gives +28% and a very flat tail) and forbids regressions elsewhere. Record the original 80% as refuted, with the evidence.

options.option: Keep the 80% target and mark G3 'behind'
options.consequence: Keeps the proposal's claim as the yardstick. G3 stays far behind indefinitely, and the goal stops being informative about progress, but the record is unambiguous about the original claim.

options.option: Keep 80%, but redefine the baseline as a weaker HTTP/3 configuration (e.g. no priority hints, single connection, older server)
options.consequence: Could make the number achievable, but only by choosing a worse opponent. It would make the result unquotable in any honest comparison; I'd advise against it.

options.option: Judge the claim refuted and retire G3, keeping G9 (speed under loss) and G10 (app-steered delivery) as the performance goals
options.consequence: Cleanest if the project's value now rests on control and predictability rather than raw p99 wins. Loses the headline metric, so the proposal's Success Metric 1 would be recorded as tested and refuted.

payload.title: A large asset streams (first chunk well before completion), a streamed body's SHA-256 matches, a mid-stream failure errors the stream rather than truncating, and a slow reader slows grants instead of growing memory without bound. Subresources stream end to end through the Service Worker.

payload.evidence: Merged main 4b594b0: npm test passes (client 72, browser 71), integrity G1 = 100 / G2 = 0, tests/demo G7 = 100. 4 MiB asset: headers 5.8 ms, first chunk 5.9 ms, complete 59 ms (65 chunks) — the consumer starts at ~10% of wall time. Slow-reader test: 16 MiB asset with a 128 KiB queue and 512 KiB budget held a peak of 574 KiB with 40 pauses and a matching SHA-256; without backpressure it would hold 16 MiB. Mid-stream failure errors the stream, and both failure paths go through one settled-guarded finish(), so a truncated body cannot close cleanly. Spike spikes/sw-stream: a ReadableStream transfers page→Service Worker on Chrome 153 (transferred stream 1.0 ms to first chunk vs 1.3 ms for posted chunks, and 48 ms vs 249 ms total on 4 MiB).

payload.title: Streaming bodies buy far less than expected: a 3 MiB module through the Service Worker is ~5% faster at 40 ms RTT and ~9% SLOWER on loopback; the real wins are time-to-first-byte and bounded memory
payload.body:
iss-x6ess8x, Chrome 153, medians of 3 alternating loads with the cache disabled:

| Path | Streaming | Buffered |
|---|---|---|
| Loopback, 3 MiB module via the worker | 247 ms | 227 ms |
| 40 ms RTT, same | 595 ms | 627 ms |

The loopback regression is real, not noise (593/595/605 vs 622/627/628 at 40 ms; the loopback runs separate similarly). Streaming compilation only pays when there is a download to overlap with; on loopback there isn't one, so all that remains is the stream machinery's per-chunk cost.

What streaming does clearly deliver:
- **Time to first byte:** on a 4 MiB asset, first chunk at 5.9 ms vs completion at 59 ms, so a consumer starts at ~10% of wall time.
- **Bounded memory under a slow reader:** a 16 MiB transfer with a 128 KiB queue held a peak of 574 KiB (40 pauses), because backpressure stops grants instead of buffering. Without it, 16 MiB.
- Small assets (4 KiB) are unaffected: 0.8 ms streamed vs 0.7 ms buffered.

So it is worth having for memory behaviour, early consumption and future compression, but it is not the fix for client-rendered page speed that fnd-ysspr7x hoped for. Default is on, with `stream: false` per session as the escape hatch.

payload.title: Streaming: transfer the ReadableStream to the Service Worker, stop grants for backpressure, emit first bytes immediately then coalesce to 64 KiB, and don't release consumed reassembly bytes
payload.body:
Implemented in iss-x6ess8x.
- **Transfer, not chunks:** Chrome 153 transfers a ReadableStream from page to Service Worker over postMessage; posting chunks instead costs ~5× (249 ms vs 48 ms on 4 MiB), so the transfer is used and no fallback is needed.
- **Backpressure stops grants:** when the stream's desiredSize ≤ 0 the transfer is paused and dropped from the grant candidates, so a slow reader stops pulling bytes off the wire rather than buffering them. Its already-granted bytes still count as outstanding, so other transfers see the truth, and the recovery timer treats it as waiting rather than stalled, so a slow reader can't fail its own transfer.
- **Chunking:** emit the first bytes immediately, then coalesce to 64 KiB (a fixed guess). Per-packet chunks produced 3,583 chunks for 4 MiB against 65 coalesced, with identical first-chunk latency.
- **Errors:** a failure after the Response was handed over errors the stream; before it, the promise rejects. Both go through one settled-guarded finish(), so a truncated body can never close cleanly.
- **Memory:** consumed bytes are not released from the reassembly buffer, because RESEND may still rewrite that region and backpressure already bounds memory.
- **Defaults:** streaming is on; `stream: false` and HEAD keep the buffered path; Content-Length comes from the declared size, since a constructed Response is not auto-decoded.

payload.title: Measure streaming on a realistic multi-asset page load, where a streamed module competes for the budget
payload.body:
From iss-x6ess8x (fnd-99zt19j). Streaming was measured on a single asset in isolation: ~5% faster at 40 ms RTT, ~9% slower on loopback. A real page is different: a streamed module competes with a dozen other transfers for one grant budget, backpressure interacts with SRPT, and the browser's parse/compile work overlaps other requests' delivery.

Fold this into the app-shape benchmark (iss-0phzwyn): run each shape with streaming on and off, at 0/50/150 ms, and report time-to-interactive. That is the measurement that decides whether streaming should stay on by default (see the default question).

payload.title: Adapt the 64 KiB chunk-coalescing threshold to the measured rate
payload.body: From iss-x6ess8x (dec-nesed3n). After the first bytes, the stream coalesces to a fixed 64 KiB. On a slow path up to 64 KiB can sit unemitted while the reader waits (completion and failure both flush, so nothing is lost, but there's an untuned latency floor). Make the threshold follow the measured delivery rate, e.g. roughly the bytes expected within a few milliseconds, bounded at both ends, and re-run the streaming measurements. Low priority.

payload.title: Deferring bulk for small requests is the design working, not a regression: at 150 ms HTTP4 wins on both axes, while on loopback it trades 17.8 MB/s of bulk for ~1 ms of latency
payload.body:
From the G3 benchmark (mea-fxsg6j2), with framing corrected after the user pointed out that slowing bulk to serve small requests is a feature.

| Condition | HTTP4 small-reply p99 | h3 | HTTP4 background | h3 background |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0% × 150 ms | **161 ms** | 225 ms | **14.2 MB/s** | 11.6 MB/s |
| clean loopback | 13.3 ms (p50 0.7) | 13.1 ms (p50 1.7) | 13.4 MB/s | **31.2 MB/s** |

At 150 ms there is no trade: SRPT wins on latency and throughput at once. On loopback the trade is real but poorly priced by a fixed policy: ~1 ms of small-reply latency bought at the cost of 58% of bulk throughput. The direction is right, the aggressiveness should not be a constant.

Implications:
- This is an argument for the priority classes in G10 (iss-j9tm9w8, iss-p891483): the app decides how hard to defer bulk, e.g. a "background" class for large transfers and "critical" for what blocks the user.
- G6 (gol-d4jyb3j, starvation) is the guardrail: deferred must not mean never. It is already failing in the worst way (fnd-g4d7cqm: a starved transfer was abandoned by its own client).
- Any scorecard should report the pair (small-reply latency, bulk throughput) together. Reporting bulk throughput alone reads as a regression when it is a deliberate allocation.

patch.body:
**Corrected 2026-09-22 after checking the code.** An earlier version of this issue said HTTP/3 sends 3–4× fewer bytes than HTTP4 on text. That is true of production HTTP/3 servers (nginx, CDNs), but NOT of our benchmark baseline: our h3 handler uses Go's http.ServeContent, which does not compress, and there is no gzip/brotli anywhere in server/. The fixture pool is also ChaCha8 random bytes, deliberately incompressible. So every comparison so far has been raw against raw, which is fair, and adding compression would not move any current benchmark.

Why it still matters: a public demo (iss-fzz5beq) is compared against real sites and real servers, where text is compressed. Uncompressed CSS/JS is then a visible, easily-measured deficit, and it also costs real bytes for real users.

Design points:
- **Negotiation:** a capability bit in HELLO (dec-cjth7tv) for the encodings the client can decode, plus `content-encoding` as an allowlisted META field (a wire change; update docs, vectors and both codecs). Without the capability the server keeps sending raw bytes, so old clients are unaffected.
- **Decoding, the practical catch:** a Response constructed in JavaScript is NOT auto-decoded, so the client must decompress. `DecompressionStream` covers gzip and deflate natively; **brotli is not available** there, so brotli needs a WASM decoder (weigh ~200 KB against ~15% over gzip). Start with gzip. This composes well with streaming bodies (dec-nesed3n), since decompression is itself a stream.
- **Server:** prefer a pre-compressed sibling (`style.css.gz`) so nothing is compressed per request; otherwise compress on the fly above a size threshold, or send raw.
- **Accounting:** total_size and the sequence numbering describe the compressed stream, while the ETag and the integrity suite's SHA-256 must keep describing the decompressed bytes. Settle this first: it touches G1's checks.

**Fair measurement is part of this issue, not an afterthought:**
- Add compressible fixtures (realistic CSS/JS-like text, and a JSON API payload) alongside the incompressible ones, with their own manifest entries.
- **Enable compression on the h3 baseline too** (gzip via a wrapping handler, or pre-compressed files with Content-Encoding). Comparing compressed HTTP4 against uncompressed h3 would flatter us the way the bench clock did (fnd-dzxejnt).
- Report transferred bytes and completion time for both stacks, compressed and not.

Acceptance: with gzip negotiated, text fixtures transfer at roughly their gzip size and decompress to bytes matching the manifest; G1 and G2 are unaffected; a browser test compares transferred bytes and times for a text-heavy page across HTTP4 and h3, both compressed; and behaviour is byte-identical to today when the capability is absent or the server flag is off.

payload.title: Neither stack compresses in our harness: the h3 baseline uses Go's ServeContent (no gzip) and the fixtures are incompressible random bytes, so every HTTP4-vs-h3 comparison so far is raw against raw
payload.body:
Checked in the code on 2026-09-22: there is no gzip, brotli or Content-Encoding anywhere in server/ (the only mention is the wire-format comment saying content-encoding is not allowed). The h3 baseline handler (server/internal/server/h3.go) serves through http.ServeContent, which does not compress; in production that job belongs to nginx or a CDN. The fixture pool is ChaCha8 random bytes, chosen so no layer can shrink them.

Consequences:
- Our comparisons are fair on this axis, and adding compression to HTTP4 alone would not change any current benchmark (random bytes don't compress), while making future text benchmarks unfair.
- Earlier statements of mine that "HTTP/3 sends 3–4× fewer bytes on text" applied to production h3 servers, not to our baseline, and should not be quoted about our measurements. iss-en0dm0f is corrected accordingly.
- Measuring compression honestly needs compressible fixtures AND compression on the h3 baseline, both now part of iss-en0dm0f.
- The gap against real-world sites is real, and shows up the moment the demo is public (iss-fzz5beq).

patch.body:
Isolated in the G3 work, 1% × 50 ms, HTTP4 p50 for small replies by background load:

| Background | HTTP4 p50 | h3 p50 |
|---|---|---|
| none | 52.0 ms (≈1 RTT) | 54.2 ms |
| 1 download | 146.6 ms (+95) | 86.6 ms (+32) |
| 4 downloads | 142.6 ms | 114.2 ms |

Alone, HTTP4 is ideal. A single competing bulk transfer costs ~95 ms, which matches quic-go's 32-datagram send queue (~38 KB) draining at the ~0.3 MB/s the lossy link allows (~125 ms). SRPT decides what to *enqueue*, but bulk datagrams already sitting in the sender's FIFO block a newly granted small reply.

**CORRECTION 2026-09-22 (from iss-dy53a59):** this finding originally attributed the whole −33.5% G3 regression at 1%×50 ms to send-queue head-of-line blocking. That is wrong. The queueing effect is real and large **on the median** (52 → 150 ms, and the pacing fix restores it to ~51 ms), but G3 scores the **p99**, and with *zero* background transfers G3 is still −22% there (HTTP4 p99 180 ms vs h3 ~147 ms). So the tail is dominated by something else, most likely loss recovery for a small reply with no following traffic to reveal the loss. See the separate finding and issue on small-reply tail loss.

The queue-drain model still explains the other conditions' medians: at 0% × 150 ms the queue drains in ~3 ms and HTTP4 wins; on loopback it is ~1–3 ms.

payload.title: HTTP4's p99 for small replies under loss is dominated by recovery, not queueing: with no competing traffic at 1%×50 ms, p99 is 180 ms vs h3's ~147 ms (G3 −22%)
payload.body:
Measured in iss-dy53a59 while validating the pacing fix, at 1% loss × 50 ms with **zero** background transfers, so no send-queue contention exists:

| | HTTP4 | h3 |
|---|---|---|
| p50 | ~52 ms (≈1 RTT) | ~54 ms |
| p99 | 180 ms | ~147 ms |

The median is ideal, so the request/grant path is right. The tail is not: a small reply is 1–4 packets, and when one is lost there is no later packet of that transfer to reveal it, and (with no other traffic) no session-wide sequence numbers either (dec-cjth7tv only helps when something follows). Recovery therefore waits for a timer of roughly 1.5–2 RTT, while QUIC detects the same loss from its own acknowledgements and retransmits sooner — which is why h3's tail is tighter on the same path.

This is the residual G3 gap under loss once the send-queue fix lands, and it scales with RTT: at 100 ms the same mechanism would add 150–200 ms to affected requests rather than 75–100.

payload.title: Cut the small-reply tail under loss: repair a 1–4 packet response without waiting for a timer (the residual G3 gap)
payload.body:
From fnd-e6ryjav. With no competing traffic at 1% × 50 ms, HTTP4's small-reply p50 is ideal (~52 ms, one RTT) but its p99 is 180 ms against h3's ~147 ms. A small reply is 1–4 packets: when one is lost there is nothing behind it to reveal the gap, session sequence numbers have nothing to compare against (dec-cjth7tv needs following traffic), and recovery falls back to a timer of ~1.5–2 RTT. QUIC detects the same loss from its acknowledgements and retransmits sooner.

Options, cheapest first:
1. **Tail redundancy:** duplicate the last packet of a small response (or send a parity packet for a 2–4 packet response). It costs one extra datagram on small replies and removes the common single-loss case entirely. Closest analogue: QUIC's tail loss probe, but proactive.
2. **Immediate tail probe:** the client re-requests the missing tail after a much tighter deadline than today's RTO when the transfer is small and the frontier has reached the grant. Cheap, but still costs a round trip.
3. **Server-side repair hint:** the server re-sends the final packet of a small RPC after ~1 RTT if no further GRANT or completion signal arrives. This moves the timer to the side that knows what it sent, though the server has no acknowledgements today.
4. **FEC across small replies:** a parity datagram over a group of small responses in the same session. More general, much more machinery, and it changes G2 accounting (parity is not granted body bytes).

Measure with `npm run bench:g3 --conditions 1x50` at bg=0 (the isolated case) plus the normal load, and report the extra bytes on the wire. Option 1's cost should be stated as a percentage of small-reply bytes.

Acceptance: at 1% × 50 ms with no background traffic, HTTP4's p99 is within ~10% of h3's, with the extra bytes quantified; no regression on clean paths.

payload.title: The pacer's latched rate estimate varies ~2× between identical runs, so it — not the send-queue depth — sets the operating point
payload.body:
Measured while sweeping the send-queue depth k for iss-dy53a59, at 1% × 50 ms with one background transfer. Raw results in the run's scratchpad (`pacer/k1-bg1.json`, `pacer/v8-bg1.json`, `pacer/iso-*.json`).

The k curve came out backwards: k=1 (the shallowest queue, which should give the tightest priority) gave a small-reply p50 of 135.6 ms, *worse* than k=4's 91.7 ms. The cause is visible in the server metrics: the pacer's latched inter-packet spacing was 1339 µs in the k=1 run against 2895 µs in the k=4 run. The pacer runs at whatever rate it latched, so a 2× swing in that estimate moves the small-reply latency far more than k does. **The k sweep as run cannot be read as a k trade-off curve.**

Why it matters beyond this sweep: the pacing change (which does fix the median, 149.7 → ~51 ms in the runs where the estimate lands well) is only as stable as an estimate that is not stable. An operating point chosen from these numbers would be chosen from noise, and a deployed pacer that latches the wrong rate is either too slow (latency on the bulk transfer) or too fast (the queueing it was meant to remove comes back).

What this does *not* explain: the p99. Across every pacing variant at bg=1 the small-reply p99 stayed 407–477 ms against h3's ~190–210 ms, even in runs where the p50 was an ideal ~51 ms. At bg=0 the same p99 is 155–180 ms against h3's 125–162 ms. So there are two separate effects — an unstable pacing rate (this finding) and a load-dependent tail — on top of the isolated recovery tail in [[fnd-e6ryjav]].

Measured at 1% × 50 ms, bg=1 (http4 p50 / p90 / p99 ms):
- unpaced baseline: 149.7 / 221.7 / 439.3, h3 p99 237.4
- paced k=4 (v8): 91.7 / 184.0 / 407.9, h3 p99 199.8
- paced k=1: 135.6 / 204.5 / 476.9, h3 p99 189.1
- best paced runs (v3/v4/v5): p50 50.8–52.4, but p99 420–471

Next: quantify the run-to-run variance of the estimate directly (repeat one configuration N times, report the spread of the latched spacing alongside the latency), then decide whether the estimator needs smoothing or a floor before any k can be chosen. See [[fnd-pp7zab7]] for the corrected attribution this sits under.

payload.title: BUG: a wildcard -wt listener advertises https://[::]:443/wt in config.json, so every deployment silently falls back to plain HTTP
payload.body:
Hit on the first real deployment (http4.armormil.com, 2026-09-22). `/config.json` served:

    {"webTransportUrl":"https://[::]:443/wt","echoUrl":"https://[::]:443/echo","h3Url":"","assetPrefix":"/"}

`[::]` is the unspecified address. No browser can dial it, so the WebTransport connect fails and every asset falls back to plain HTTP — the demo looks like it works, and the panel reports `fallback` for everything. Nothing in the logs says anything is wrong, which is what makes this bad: the failure is silent and the page still renders.

Cause, `server/internal/server/server.go:201`:

    WebTransportURL: "https://" + cmp.Or(cfg.AdvertiseWT, udpConn.LocalAddr().String()) + WebTransportPath,

With `-wt :443` (the documented way to listen on all interfaces) `udpConn.LocalAddr()` is `[::]:443`, and that goes straight into the advertised URL. `-advertise-wt host:port` works around it, but it is described in the flag help as a testing knob for putting an impairment proxy in front, so nothing tells a deployer they need it. QUICKSTART.md does not mention it either.

Fix: `/config.json` is served per request by `handleConfig`, so the server already knows the host the browser used. When the WT listener's host is unspecified (`::`, `0.0.0.0`, or empty), build the advertised URL from the request's `Host` with the WT listener's port, instead of from the listen address. `-advertise-wt` keeps overriding everything, unchanged. A concrete host in `-wt` keeps being used as today.

Care needed: the request Host is attacker-controlled, so it must not be echoed anywhere it could do harm — here it only comes back to the same client in its own config, which is the same trust level as the page it was served from, but the port must come from the listener rather than from Host, and a Host with no valid hostname should fall back to today's behaviour rather than emit something malformed.

Also: make this visible rather than silent. At startup, log the advertised WebTransport URL, and warn plainly if it contains an unspecified address. The deploy check in QUICKSTART.md should include reading `config.json` back and confirming the host is the real one.

Acceptance: a server started with a wildcard `-wt` and no `-advertise-wt` serves a `config.json` whose `webTransportUrl` names the host the request arrived on; a test covers `::`, `0.0.0.0` and a concrete host, with and without `-advertise-wt`; QUICKSTART.md's verification step checks the advertised host.

payload.title: The pacer's blocked-send clock is unsound: quic-go's queue unblocks after one departure, which is indistinguishable from a descheduled send
payload.body:
Supersedes [[fnd-ey1vr9d]], which said the latched rate estimate merely "varies ~2× between runs". The mechanism is worse than variance, and it is one-directional.

**Why the clock is unsound.** The pacer infers the wire's departure rate from sends that blocked, on the premise that a block means the queue is full, so between two blocked sends exactly as many datagrams left as were handed over. In quic-go v0.63 (`datagram_queue.go`) `Add` blocks only while `Len() >= 32` and is released by the next `Pop` — so a genuine block lasts about *one departure interval*, a few ms on this path. That is the same order as an ordinary send that was merely descheduled on a loaded host. Wall-clock duration cannot separate the two. So sample endpoints are sometimes taken when the queue was *not* full, and the error can only run one way: too many sends counted against the interval, so the wire always looks faster than it is. Measured over-count in steady state: 1.4–3.7×.

**How bad in practice.** In an instrumented run, **113 of 114 samples were rejected by the saturation gate, and the single accepted sample (986 µs, taken during slow-start warm-up) governed the entire run.** The estimate is therefore set by one unrepresentative measurement taken before the connection reached steady state, and never revised.

**Mitigation landed:** keep the *slowest* well-blocked sample in a 5 s window rather than an average, since the contamination is one-directional and the slowest sample is the least contaminated. This makes the estimator usable, not sound.

**The sound fix, not yet built:** the receiver already tells the sender how fast bytes are actually arriving, every round trip, in the advance of its GRANTs. That is a direct measurement of goodput at the only place that observes it, needs no inference from send-call timing, and cannot be contaminated by host scheduling. A future estimator should take its rate from the GRANT advance rather than from blocked sends.

Correcting the reference rate used earlier in this investigation: the wire's true departure interval at 1% × 50 ms with one background transfer is ~2817 µs (from the server's own `data_packets` over the window), not the ~4500 µs or ~7000 µs inferred from `backgroundMBps` — see [[fnd-2h3ndiq]] for why that metric misled. Against 2817 µs, k=4's latched 2895 µs was within 3%, while k=1's 1339 µs was 2.1× too fast and genuinely wrong. The k1/k2/k8 numbers are therefore not a k curve: k was not the variable, the latched rate was.

payload.title: backgroundMBps counts only completed transfers, so it is quantized to whole 10 MiB units and cannot show a throughput difference
payload.body:
`client/bench/bench.ts:231` accumulates background bytes as `st.bytes += await fetchBytes(...)`, so bytes are added only when a fetch *resolves*. A transfer still in flight when the window ends is aborted, throws, and contributes **nothing** — and every G3 run ends with `aborted: 1`.

The consequence is that `background.bytes` is always an exact multiple of the fixture size. Every run in the pacing investigation reported exactly 10485760 bytes — one whole 10 MiB transfer — and therefore 0.167–0.170 MB/s in *every* variant, paced and unpaced, at every k. **The metric is structurally incapable of resolving a difference smaller than one complete transfer**, so identical values across variants carry no information at all.

I read that flatness as evidence that pacing costs no bulk throughput, and said so twice. It was wrong. The server's own counters tell a very different story for the same condition (1% × 50 ms, bg=1), in payload MB moved over the window:

- unpaced: 23.9
- pacing from the fastest sample: 23.7
- gated + headroom: 21.0
- EWMA: 16.1
- pacing from the slowest sample: 10.6

That is a range of better than 2×, entirely invisible in `backgroundMBps`. The trade-off the k sweep existed to price is real and large.

The same error corrupted the reference rate: dividing the censored byte count by the window gave ~4500 µs (and, before accounting for foreground traffic, ~7000 µs) per datagram, against a true ~2817 µs from `data_packets`. That made the pacer look inert when it was in fact binding — `paced_wait_micros` is 33–60 s against 0 in the unpaced arm.

**Rule this establishes:** derive bench throughput from the server's `data_packets`/`data_bytes` counters over the measured window, never from completed-transfer counts on the client. A partial transfer's bytes are real bytes on the wire and must be counted. See [[fnd-3djsbd7]] for the estimator this misled, and the issue that fixes the metric.

payload.title: BUG: bench background throughput drops the in-flight transfer's bytes; take throughput from the server's counters instead
payload.body:
From [[fnd-02seb49]]. `client/bench/bench.ts:231` does `st.bytes += await fetchBytes(...)`, so only a fetch that *resolves* contributes. The transfer in flight when the window closes is aborted, throws, and its bytes are discarded — and every G3 run ends with `aborted: 1`.

`background.bytes` is therefore always an exact multiple of the fixture size, and `backgroundMBps` cannot resolve any difference smaller than one whole 10 MiB transfer. It reported 0.167–0.170 MB/s across every pacing variant while the server's counters showed 10.6–23.9 MB moved — a better-than-2× spread, completely hidden. This actively misled the pacing investigation in two directions at once (throughput looked flat, and the derived wire rate was ~1.6× too slow).

Fix:
- Count partial bytes: have `fetchBytes` report progress, or accumulate as chunks arrive, so an aborted transfer's bytes still land in the total.
- Better, and needed regardless: report throughput from the server's `data_bytes` / `data_packets` delta across the measured window, which counts what actually went on the wire including resends, and add it to the G3 output alongside the client's view. Report both, since a gap between them is itself informative (resends, loss).
- Keep `completed` / `aborted` as they are; the bug is only in the byte total.

Acceptance: a G3 run at 1% × 50 ms with one background transfer reports a background throughput that changes when the pacing rate changes, agrees with `data_bytes`/window to within the resend overhead, and is no longer an exact multiple of the fixture size. Re-state [[fnd-02seb49]]'s numbers from the corrected metric.

payload.title: Ship sender pacing switched off by default: no pacing rate improves the p99 that G3 scores, and every rate that helps the median costs bulk throughput
payload.body:
Decided from the pacing-rate sweep at 1% × 50 ms with one background transfer (iss-dy53a59), once [[fnd-3djsbd7]] (the unsound rate clock) and [[fnd-02seb49]] (the censored throughput metric) were corrected and throughput was taken from the server's counters. Slot interval → small-reply p50 / p99 in ms, and bulk as a percentage of the unpaced arm:

| slot µs | p50 | p99 | bulk |
|---|---|---|---|
| unpaced | 149.7 | 439.3 | 100% |
| 2442 | 117.3 | 424.0 | 99% |
| 2895 | 91.7 | 407.9 | 88% |
| 3732 | 50.8 | 420.4 | 67% |
| 4827 | 51.5 | 561.0 | 44% |

One smooth monotone curve once the rate — not k — is the variable, which is itself the evidence that the earlier k1/k2/k8 numbers were noise.

**Why off by default.** The median improves a lot (149.7 → 50.8 ms, three round trips down to one) but only by giving up a third of bulk throughput, and **no setting improves the p99 that G3 actually scores** — the best paced p99 (407.9) is barely under the unpaced 439.3, and the setting that fixes the median makes the p99 *worse* at the shallow end (561.0 at 4827 µs). There is no operating point that wins on both, and the goal G3 is written against the p99. Shipping a default that trades a third of throughput for a metric the project does not score would be choosing the number that looks good over the one that was committed to.

**What ships:** the mechanism, its tests, and `-send-queue k` to opt in. Users who care about small-reply latency more than bulk throughput can set it; the default path is byte-identical to before. This keeps the work and the measurement without imposing the trade.

**What this leaves open:** the p99 under loss is still unexplained and is the real G3 gap — see [[fnd-e6ryjav]] (a small reply of 1–4 packets has nothing following it to reveal a loss) and iss-px7fmgg. Pacing was the wrong tree; loss recovery is the right one. A sound rate estimator built on the GRANT advance ([[fnd-3djsbd7]]) would be needed before pacing could be reconsidered as a default.

payload.title: G3 at 1% × 50 ms is a ratio against an h3 baseline that varies up to 3× between runs, so cross-run G3 comparisons at that condition are not reliable
payload.body:
Found while verifying that the pacing branch's default path matches main (iss-dy53a59). With pacing off, **http4's own numbers are unchanged** — p50 145.6 vs main's 146.6, p99 481.7 vs 448.5, inside the spread of a repeat of main itself at 490.4. But the reported G3 moved substantially between those runs, and the movement came entirely from the **baseline**: h3's p99 went 424.3 → 303.2 ms.

Across every run collected in this investigation, h3's p99 at 1% × 50 ms ranged roughly 144–424 ms. G3 is defined as an improvement ratio against that baseline, so a 3× swing in the denominator dominates any effect a change to http4 might have. **The headline "G3 = −33.5% at 1% × 50 ms" cannot be compared against a G3 measured in a different run.**

Note the structure of the noise: *within* a run the five repeats are tight (e.g. h3 perRepeatP99 = 222.1, 168.2, 173.4, 181.3, 177.2), while *between* runs the spread is large. So this is not sampling noise — something differs per run and stays fixed for its duration.

A likely confound, visible in the data: in the run where h3's p99 was worst (424.3) the h3 arm's background transfer never completed, while in better runs it did. Whether the 10 MiB background transfer finishes inside the window changes how much contention the foreground samples actually see, and that differs per run and per stack. The censored byte counter ([[fnd-02seb49]]) hid this, because a transfer that did not complete reported the same total as one that never started.

Consequences:
- Any G3 figure must be quoted with the run it came from, and G3 changes smaller than the baseline's spread mean nothing.
- The pacing conclusions in [[dec-ckarh9c]] rest on *within-run* comparisons across pacing rates, which are not affected by this. The cross-run claim "the default path matches main" rests on http4's absolute numbers, which are also unaffected.
- The earlier attribution work ([[fnd-pp7zab7]], [[fnd-e6ryjav]]) compared http4 and h3 inside the same run, so it stands, but its *magnitudes* inherit the baseline's variability.

Fix direction: interleave the stacks within a repeat rather than running each stack's full window in sequence, so both see the same machine and path state; hold the background workload identical across stacks (which requires the byte-counting fix, iss-fky86ta); and report G3 with a spread across repeats rather than a single number, refusing to quote a difference smaller than that spread.

sources.note: pacing-off verification vs main; h3 p99 424.3 -> 303.2 between runs, ~144-424 across all runs at 1x50

payload.title: Make G3 comparable across runs: interleave the stacks, equalise the background workload, and report a spread instead of one number
payload.body:
From [[fnd-q7mn3zg]]. G3 scores the project's headline claim, but at 1% × 50 ms its h3 baseline varied roughly 144–424 ms across runs while http4's own numbers stayed put. A metric defined as a ratio against that baseline cannot support the cross-run comparisons it is being used for.

The noise is structured, not random: within a run the five repeats are tight, between runs the spread is large. So something is fixed per run and differs between them.

Work:
1. **Interleave the stacks.** Today each stack runs its whole window in sequence, so http4 and h3 see the machine and the path at different times. Alternate them within a repeat (or randomise the order and report it) so both meet the same conditions.
2. **Equalise the background workload.** In the worst baseline run the h3 arm's background transfer never completed, so its foreground samples saw different contention from a run where it did. Depends on the byte-counting fix (iss-fky86ta), since the censored counter made a transfer that never completed look identical to one that did.
3. **Report a spread.** Emit G3 with a per-repeat distribution and a confidence interval, and make the tooling refuse to quote a difference smaller than the baseline's own spread. A single G3 number without its spread should not appear in the output at all.
4. **Re-measure the headline.** Once the above lands, re-run the official G3 and supersede mea-fxsg6j2 / [[fnd-xj391f2]] with numbers that carry their uncertainty. The current −33.5% at 1% × 50 ms should be treated as provisional until then.

Acceptance: two consecutive `npm run bench:g3` runs with no code change between them produce G3 values whose intervals overlap, and the reported h3 baseline p99 differs between them by less than the reported spread. The output names the run and carries the interval alongside every G3 figure.

payload.title: Re-clock the pacer on the receiver's GRANT advance, the only path to turning pacing on by default
payload.body:
From [[fnd-3djsbd7]] and [[dec-ckarh9c]]. The pacing mechanism is landed and correct but ships off, and the blocker is the rate estimate, not the mechanism.

Today the sender infers the wire's departure rate from sends that blocked. That clock is unsound: quic-go's `Add` unblocks after a single `Pop`, which on this path is a few milliseconds — the same order as a send merely descheduled on a loaded host. The two cannot be told apart by wall-clock duration, and the resulting miscount runs only one way (too many sends, so the wire looks faster than it is). In an instrumented run 113 of 114 samples were rejected and the single accepted one was taken during slow start, governing the whole run. The mitigation (keep the slowest well-blocked sample in a 5 s window) makes it usable, not sound.

**The receiver already measures the thing we want.** It grants byte ceilings every round trip, and the rate at which its grants advance *is* the rate bytes are actually arriving — measured at the only place that observes delivery, needing no inference from send-call timing, and immune to host scheduling on the sender.

Work:
- Derive the sender's pacing rate from the advance of each session's GRANTs over time rather than from blocked sends. Consider whether it is per-RPC or session-wide (session-wide is what the pacer needs, since the queue is shared).
- Handle the cases where the signal is absent or stale: a paused receiver (grants stop but the wire is fine), a receiver whose budget is capped rather than rate-limited, and start-up before any grant has advanced. Falling back to today's behaviour is acceptable; silently pacing to a stale rate is not.
- Keep the mechanism and `-send-queue` as they are; only the rate source changes.
- Re-run the rate sweep with the new clock. The question to answer is whether a sound rate lands somewhere the current curve could not reach — in particular whether the p99 improves at all, since [[dec-ckarh9c]] turned pacing off because no rate did.

Acceptance: the latched rate tracks the measured wire rate (from server `data_bytes` over the window, per iss-fky86ta) within ~10% across repeated runs at 1% × 50 ms, instead of varying 2×; the rate sweep is re-run and recorded; and the default-on question is re-decided on the new numbers rather than assumed.

payload.title: Small-reply p50 with 1 background transfer within ~20 ms of the no-background p50 (52 ms)

payload.evidence: At k=4, 1% x 50 ms: 50.8 ms with one background transfer, against 51.8 ms with none (before, same binary with -send-queue -1: 149.7 ms). Sender-level test confirms the mechanism: bulk datagrams queued ahead of a small reply drop from 34 to 1-3. Requires opting in with -send-queue 4; the shipped default is off.

payload.title: G3 at 1% x 50 ms is no longer negative

payload.evidence: Not met, and unreachable by this route. At ZERO background transfers G3 at 1x50 is already -21.9%, so send-queue head-of-line blocking was never what made G3 negative (fnd-pp7zab7's attribution was wrong; see fnd-e6ryjav). No pacing rate improves the p99 that G3 scores: unpaced 439.3 ms, best paced 407.9 ms, and the rate that fixes the median makes it worse at 561.0 ms (dec-ckarh9c). The residual gap is loss recovery on 1-4 packet replies, tracked in iss-px7fmgg. Note also that G3 at this condition divides by an h3 baseline that varies up to 3x between runs (fnd-q7mn3zg), so the figure itself needs iss-15jdad0 before it can be trusted.
