payload.evidence: Met, though trivially: pacing never engages below 250 us/datagram (pacerMinInterval), and a clean loopback path is far faster than that, so the pacer is inert there. Confirmed by the integrity suite reporting paced_waits: 0 on the shipped default. Note this criterion was easy for the wrong reason -- the real throughput cost is on LOSSY paths, where the rate that fixes the median costs about a third of bulk (dec-ckarh9c), which is why the default is off.

payload.title: Three traps made a working HTTP4 deployment look broken, and all three fail silently by falling back to plain HTTP
payload.body:
First real deployment (http4.armormil.com, an LXC container on a Proxmox homelab behind pfSense, 2026-09-22/23). The server, protocol and LAN were correct the whole time. Verified from a LAN host: QUIC handshake 11–80 ms, WebTransport session HTTP 200.

Three independent faults, each of which produces the *identical* symptom — the panel reports `fallback` for every resource and the page renders perfectly, with nothing in any log saying anything is wrong:

1. **Wildcard listener advertised as a dialable address.** `-wt :443` makes `config.json` advertise `https://[::]:443/wt`. No browser can dial the unspecified address. Fixed at the time with `-advertise-wt host:port`; the code fix is iss-07wbk3k.

2. **A typo in `-origin`.** Only *loopback* origins are auto-allowed (`server.go:383`); a public hostname must be listed exactly. `https://http4.armomil.com` (a missing letter) means the browser's real origin is not in the allowlist, and the upgrade is rejected with 403. Confirmed live: the same probe got 403 with `Origin: https://192.168.22.193` and 200 with `Origin: https://http4.armormil.com`.

3. **NAT hairpin, which also invalidates the obvious test.** A client *inside* the network resolving the public hostname gets the public IP and needs NAT reflection to reach the server. TCP hairpinned fine while UDP did not, so the page loaded and WebTransport timed out. Worse, those packets never reach the WAN interface, so a `tcpdump` on WAN shows nothing and looks like an upstream block. **Testing a public deployment from inside its own NAT proves nothing.** The fix for LAN clients is split DNS (resolve the hostname to the internal address) rather than NAT reflection.

A methodological note worth keeping: I diagnosed (3) as an ISP/firewall problem and had the operator capture on WAN, having never checked my own vantage point — my "external" probe ran on a host at `192.168.16.252`, inside the same NAT, behind the same gateway that appeared in the server's own logs. Validating the instrument against Cloudflare and Google proved outbound UDP worked, but that is internal→internet, a different path from internal→own-public-IP, so it confirmed nothing about the case at hand. **Before trusting a reachability probe, establish where it is running relative to the thing being probed.**

Still open and genuinely unknown: whether inbound UDP 443 reaches the WAN from the internet at all. Every test so far was from inside.

sources.note: live deployment; QUIC handshake 11-80 ms and WebTransport HTTP 200 from a LAN host to the container

payload.title: Add a deploy doctor and rewrite QUICKSTART's troubleshooting: every deployment fault currently fails silently as "fallback"
payload.body:
From [[fnd-w68x5w7]]. Three independent faults in the first real deployment each produced the same symptom — `fallback` on every resource, a page that renders perfectly, and nothing in any log. Diagnosing them took hours and several wrong turns. None of it should have needed a human.

**1. `http4d doctor` (or `serve -check`), run from the server:**
- Warn loudly at startup when the advertised WebTransport URL contains an unspecified address (`::`, `0.0.0.0`) — see iss-07wbk3k. This alone would have caught fault 1 immediately.
- Warn when `-origin` is set but does not contain the origin implied by `-domain`, which catches the typo class directly. A near-miss (small edit distance) should say so explicitly: "no origin matches `-domain http4.armormil.com`; did you mean the given `https://http4.armomil.com`?"
- Dial its own advertised WebTransport URL and report whether the session establishes, with the failure named (timeout → UDP not reaching; 403 → origin rejected).
- Report the UDP receive buffer and whether the kernel granted what QUIC asked for, noting that in a container this is set on the host (`net.core.rmem_max` is not network-namespaced).

**2. A client-visible reason.** The panel says `fallback` with no cause. It should carry why the session failed — connect timeout, 403, certificate — since that single word is the operator's main signal and it currently discards everything useful.

**3. QUICKSTART troubleshooting rewrite:**
- **Never test a public deployment from inside its own NAT.** Hairpinned UDP commonly fails where TCP succeeds, and those packets never reach the WAN interface, so a WAN capture shows nothing and looks exactly like an upstream block. Use a phone on cellular, or a host elsewhere.
- Split DNS (resolve the hostname to the internal address) is the fix for LAN clients, not NAT reflection.
- TCP 443 and UDP 443 are separate firewall rules. A TCP-mode proxy such as HAProxy cannot carry QUIC at all, so the UDP path must bypass it.
- On iOS every browser is WebKit, so a phone test may show `fallback` for lack of WebTransport rather than any network fault. Say how to check (`typeof WebTransport`).
- Verify the deployment by reading `config.json` back and confirming the advertised host is the real one.

Acceptance: `http4d doctor` against a server with each of the three faults injected names the fault and the fix in one line each; the panel shows a reason alongside `fallback`; QUICKSTART's troubleshooting section covers the NAT, split-DNS, UDP-rule and WebKit traps.

payload.title: First real-network page-load comparison: HTTP4 is 16% slower to LCP and 57% slower to load, delivering ~16 MiB/s against HTTP/2's ~75 MiB/s on a LAN path
payload.body:
Two Chrome DevTools traces of the live demo (http4.armormil.com, LXC container on a Proxmox homelab, client on a different subnet across pfSense), captured 40 s apart on 2026-09-23: `?http4=off` (HTTP/2 over TCP) versus HTTP4. Same page, same 6.19 MiB of content, 21 unique URLs each. **This is the first measurement of HTTP4 on real network infrastructure rather than loopback or the impairment proxy.**

| metric | HTTP/2 | HTTP4 | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| DOMContentLoaded | 1092.2 ms | 1278.4 ms | +186.2 |
| FCP / LCP | 1127.7 ms | 1305.9 ms | **+178.2 (+15.8%)** |
| loadEventEnd | 1168.7 ms | 1832.9 ms | **+664.2 (+56.8%)** |
| last resource finish | 1178.1 ms | 1844.4 ms | +666.3 |
| main-thread busy | 332 ms | 572 ms | +240 |

**1. SRPT works exactly as specified.** HTTP4's twelve images complete in strict ascending size order, with no exceptions: 150 KiB at 1292 ms, 222 at 1304, 276 at 1325, 319 at 1348, 364 at 1369, 422 at 1392, 515 at 1423, 579 at 1467, 646 at 1503, 798 at 1550, 894 at 1598, 1053 at 1832. HTTP/2's completion order is unrelated to size (894 KiB finishes at 1103 ms, 150 KiB at 1139). The scheduler is doing precisely what it claims.

**2. Connection setup costs ~180 ms and explains the whole LCP regression.** HTTP4's first subresource byte arrives at 1257 ms against HTTP/2's 1077 ms. Nothing can move until `auto.js` loads (finishes 1076 ms), then `config.json` (1085 ms), then the WebTransport session establishes. Every subresource shows a TTFB clustered at 1257–1259 ms — they all unblock at the same instant, when the session comes up. The LCP delta (+178 ms) is almost exactly this startup cost. This is the known "every page load reconnects" caveat, now measured on a real path.

**3. Throughput is 4–5× lower.** Sustained delivery is 0.69–0.90 MiB per 50 ms window (≈14–18 MiB/s) against HTTP/2's peak of 3.73 MiB per 50 ms (≈75 MiB/s). HTTP/2 moved the entire 6.19 MiB in a ~150 ms window; HTTP4 needed ~590 ms. On a fast, uncongested LAN this is the dominant cost and it is not explained by JS CPU (see 5).

**4. A ~100 ms delivery stall near the end.** Nothing arrives between 1650 and 1750 ms, then delivery resumes for the last 0.53 MiB. This falls on `lagoon.png`, the largest asset (1053 KiB), whose completion sits 234 ms past the trend line the other eleven follow. Worth investigating — it resembles the starvation pattern in iss-6p9cq3q, and it is the single largest contributor to the load-time gap after the throughput difference.

**5. Not CPU-bound in JavaScript.** Main-thread busy time is up (332 → 572 ms) and the thread runs 60–92% busy through the transfer, but the CPU profile attributes only tens of milliseconds to client JS (`readLoop` 11.9 ms, `handle` 6.3 ms). An initial reading suggested 6.6 s in `http4-sw.js`; that was wrong — profile node IDs collide across threads, and merging them mislabelled the `(idle)` frame. Split per thread it is idle. So the throughput gap is in delivery, not in client processing.

**Caveats, which matter here.** One run per stack, no repeats, taken 40 s apart. [[fnd-q7mn3zg]] established that the h3 baseline at a *controlled* condition varies up to 3× between runs, so single-run deltas on an uncontrolled path should be treated as indicative, not settled. More importantly, **a fast uncongested LAN is HTTP4's least favourable condition**: its entire value proposition is allocating scarce capacity by priority, and there is nothing scarce here to allocate. The interesting comparison is a constrained or lossy path, which this is not.

payload.title: Find why HTTP4 sustains only ~16 MiB/s on a LAN path where HTTP/2 reaches ~75 MiB/s
payload.body:
From [[fnd-jek9y6q]], the first real-network measurement. Delivering the demo's 6.19 MiB took HTTP4 ~590 ms against HTTP/2's ~150 ms. Sustained HTTP4 delivery was 0.69–0.90 MiB per 50 ms (≈14–18 MiB/s); HTTP/2 peaked at 3.73 MiB per 50 ms (≈75 MiB/s). Client JS is not the bottleneck — the CPU profile attributes only tens of milliseconds to it.

This matters beyond the demo: it is a ceiling that shows up on any fast path, and it is invisible in the impairment-proxy benchmarks because those deliberately constrain the path far below it.

Hypotheses to separate, cheapest first:
1. **Grant cadence.** The budget is `clamp(2 × maxRate × minRtt, 128 KiB, 16 MiB)`, so on a sub-millisecond LAN RTT it floors at 128 KiB. If grants are issued on a timer rather than on arrival, the achieved rate is 128 KiB per tick regardless of the wire. 16 MiB/s ÷ 128 KiB ≈ 128 grant cycles/s ≈ 7.8 ms per cycle — suspiciously close to a timer interval, and nowhere near a LAN RTT. **Check this first**: instrument the interval between successive GRANTs and the bytes each one opens.
2. **Serialization under SRPT.** Strict shortest-remaining-first means one transfer holds the budget at a time, so there is no cross-asset pipelining to fill the pipe while one transfer waits for its next grant. HTTP/2 has a dozen streams in flight absorbing the same latency.
3. **Datagram overhead.** 6.19 MiB at 1183-byte payloads is ~5,500 datagrams, each crossing the browser's WebTransport datagram path individually. Measure the per-datagram cost directly rather than assuming it.
4. **The 128 KiB budget floor itself.** If the floor is what binds on fast paths, it is the wrong floor; it should scale with observed delivery rate rather than sit at a constant chosen for slow links.

Measure with the demo page against the live server (or a local server with no impairment), reporting: GRANT interval distribution, bytes granted per cycle, achieved MiB/s, and datagrams/second. Compare against HTTP/2 on the identical path.

Acceptance: the dominant cause is identified with evidence, and either fixed or recorded as an accepted limit with the reason. If it is (1) or (4), fixing it should raise LAN throughput materially without hurting the lossy-path behaviour the impairment matrix covers — verify both.

payload.title: On a slow link the HTTP4 client bootstraps too late to carry anything: 0.0% of bytes over HTTP4 at 3G, against 98.9% on the LAN
payload.body:
Two further DevTools traces of the live demo under DevTools network throttling ("3G": 50,000 B/s each way, 2000 ms latency), 2026-09-23, one with `?http4=off` and one without.

**The two traces are indistinguishable** — FCP 6476.2 vs 6439.1 ms, load 134504.0 vs 134384.1 ms, last resource 136527.5 vs 136407.2 ms. A 0.09% difference across 134 seconds. The reason is not that the transports perform alike; it is that **HTTP4 was never used**.

Bytes actually carried, by whether the resource had a real network fetch or was served by the Service Worker with no network twin:

| | over HTTP4 | over plain HTTP | share |
|---|---|---|---|
| LAN (earlier trace) | 6269.8 KiB | 67.6 KiB | **98.9%** |
| 3G | 1.0 KiB | 6340.5 KiB | **0.0%** |

At 3G only the three small API JSONs (451 + 449 + 78 B) went over HTTP4. Every image, the stylesheet, the script and the font fell back.

**Why, from the timeline.** The bootstrap is serialized and slow, while the page's subresources are dispatched immediately:

- `index.html` finishes 3118.9 ms
- the browser dispatches all twelve images at **3118.7 ms** — the Service Worker intercepts them, has no session, and falls back
- `auto.js` (63.9 KiB, ~1.3 s at 50 KB/s on its own) finishes 6387.1 ms
- `config.json` finishes 8395.9 ms — it cannot start until `auto.js` has run
- the WebTransport session comes up after that, ~8.4 s in
- `app.js` later fetches the three API JSONs at 10573 ms, by which time the session exists, so those three go over HTTP4

So the client becomes useful roughly 5 seconds after the requests it was meant to carry have already been issued. **The benefit arrives too late to apply precisely on the links where it would matter most**, because the bootstrap cost is itself paid over the slow link.

Two structural causes, both fixable:
1. **The bootstrap is a serial chain over the slow link**: HTML → `auto.js` (63.9 KiB) → `config.json` → handshake. Three round trips plus a large script before the first HTTP4 byte can move.
2. **Fallback is immediate.** The Service Worker falls back the instant it has no session, rather than holding a request briefly for one that is moments away.

**Caveat on the method, which matters for future runs.** Because nothing traversed WebTransport here, these traces do *not* establish whether DevTools throttling applies to WebTransport datagrams at all. If it does not, a 3G comparison in which HTTP4 *did* work would unfairly favour HTTP4 — its traffic would be unthrottled while HTTP/2's is capped. That must be verified before trusting any future DevTools-throttled comparison. Impairing the path outside the browser (netem on the host, or the project's own `impair` proxy applied to both stacks) avoids the question entirely.

Supersedes nothing, but note it reframes [[fnd-jek9y6q]]: that LAN comparison was a genuine HTTP4-vs-HTTP/2 measurement (98.9% carried), this one is not.

payload.title: Cut the HTTP4 bootstrap to one round trip, and hold requests briefly instead of falling back instantly (today a slow link gets 0% over HTTP4)
payload.body:
From [[fnd-sgw2sbh]]. At DevTools 3G the demo carried **0.0%** of its bytes over HTTP4 — 1.0 KiB of 6.3 MiB — because the client is not ready until ~8.4 s, while the browser dispatches every image at 3.1 s. On the LAN the same page carries 98.9%. The library therefore helps least exactly where it would help most.

Two independent causes, addressable separately.

**A. The bootstrap is a serial chain over the slow link.** HTML → `auto.js` (63.9 KiB) → `config.json` → WebTransport handshake. Three round trips plus a large script, all before the first HTTP4 byte.
1. **Inline the config.** Serve the WebTransport URL (and cert hash in dev) in the HTML the client is already parsing — a `<script type="application/json">` block or a data attribute on the existing tag — removing a whole round trip. Keep `/config.json` as the fallback so nothing breaks.
2. **Let the Service Worker bootstrap itself.** The SW is already installed and controlling from a previous visit; it does not need to wait for the page's `auto.js` to tell it anything. It can fetch its config and open the session at activation, in parallel with the navigation, so the session is often ready before the first subresource arrives.
3. **Shrink `auto.js`.** 63.9 KiB is ~1.3 s at 50 KB/s on its own. Split the part needed to open a session from the rest (panel, stats, fallback plumbing), and load the remainder lazily. Report the before/after byte count.
4. Consider `<link rel="preconnect">`-style warming, and whether the session can be opened from the HTML's `<head>` before subresources are dispatched.

**B. Fallback is instantaneous and irreversible.** The SW falls back the moment it finds no session. On a slow link that decision is made ~5 s before the session exists, and cannot be revisited.
5. **Hold briefly.** When a session is establishing, hold an interceptable request for a short, bounded window (tens of ms, tuned; possibly scaled by the request's priority) before falling back. A request held 50 ms that then rides HTTP4 beats one dispatched immediately over a congested HTTP/1-style path — but only if the wait is bounded and the fallback still fires reliably. Measure both directions; this can easily make things worse.
6. The hold must never apply when there is no prospect of a session (WebTransport unsupported, previous connect failed), or first paint pays for nothing.

**Measurement.** Report "% of bytes over HTTP4" directly in the demo panel — it is the number that would have made this obvious immediately, and today the panel shows only per-resource `fallback` labels. Then re-run the app-shape benchmark (iss-0phzwyn) at 50/150 ms RTT and a bandwidth cap, and check the share at each.

**Do not measure this with DevTools throttling** until it is established whether that throttling applies to WebTransport datagrams at all (see [[fnd-sgw2sbh]]). Use netem on the host or the `impair` proxy applied to both stacks.

Acceptance: on a link slow enough that the page takes >10 s, the share of bytes over HTTP4 is a large majority rather than ~0, with the bootstrap's round trips and bytes reported before and after; and no regression in first paint on a fast path.

payload.title: A page carries its HTTP4 config inline by hand; the server does not inject it
payload.body:
For iss-rba9103. The client now reads an optional `<script type="application/http4-config">` block from the page, skipping the `/config.json` round trip that cannot start until `auto.js` has run.

**Why not have the server inject it**, which would have been zero-config for any site: in `serve` mode every path is *also* an HTTP4 asset, including `index.html`. Rewriting `text/html` on the way out would make the page served over HTTP differ from the same file served over HTTP4 and from its on-disk SHA-256, and would require recomputing `Content-Length`, `ETag` and `Range` handling. Trading byte-identity for a round trip is a bad exchange in a project whose first goal (G1) is that delivered bytes match.

**Why not a `Link: rel=preload` header**, the other non-mutating option: it would only parallelise the fetch rather than remove it, and the client requests `/config.json` with `cache: "no-store"`, which would likely bypass the preload cache — so it would need that relaxed to work at all, for a smaller benefit.

**What was chosen:** the site author writes the block. No server change, nothing to build, and it ships immediately. The cost is that it is manual and must be kept in step with `-advertise-wt`.

Consequences accepted, all documented in `examples/demo-site/README.md`:
- **A wrong `webTransportUrl` is used, not validated.** The session fails to connect and the page runs fallback-only; it does not quietly re-read `/config.json`. This is the sharp edge.
- **Trusted certificates only.** A dev certificate's `certHash` changes every run, so development servers must keep using `/config.json`.
- **A malformed block is harmless** — invalid JSON, empty, or missing `webTransportUrl` falls back to fetching `/config.json`, costing the round trip back rather than the session.
- **The demo site ships no inline block**, deliberately: a hardcoded URL would pin it to one deployment and break `bin/http4d serve` locally.

Revisit if the manual step proves error-prone in practice, or if the measurement under netem (rather than DevTools throttling, whose applicability to WebTransport is unverified — [[fnd-sgw2sbh]]) shows the round trip is not actually material.

payload.title: The worker's wait for a session scales with what is waiting on the bytes: 400 ms for render-blocking, 6 s for bulk
payload.body:
For iss-rba9103 and the first step of iss-pp8s2ym. The Service Worker already held a request up to `READY_TIMEOUT_MS` (2 s) waiting for its tab's HTTP4 session, but applied one number to everything. At DevTools 3G the session came up ~8.4 s in, so every image timed out and fell back, and the page carried **0%** of its bytes over HTTP4 ([[fnd-sgw2sbh]]).

**The reasoning that sets the numbers.** Holding is an asymmetric bet. Nothing has been requested yet when the worker holds, so a hold that ends in fallback costs *exactly its own length* in pure delay — but a hold that pays off puts those bytes under the scheduler, which is the entire point of the protocol. The right wait therefore depends on what the delay costs, which depends on what is waiting on the bytes:

| destination | wait | why |
|---|---|---|
| `style`, `script` | 400 ms | render-blocking; every millisecond held is a millisecond of first paint |
| `image`, `video`, `audio` | 6000 ms | nothing paints sooner, they arrive in bulk, they are what SRPT exists to order — and they are exactly the requests the browser dispatches earliest and the session misses on a slow link |
| everything else | 2000 ms | unchanged: `font` (text is already laid out), `""` for fetch/XHR (the app is running, so a session is normally up), and anything new |

These are **caps on a wait, not delays that are actually spent**: the wait ends early whenever the tab's connect attempt resolves either way, bounded by `connectTimeoutMs` (5 s by default). So the 6 s image cap is only approached when a connect is genuinely slow, and a *failed* connect releases every held request at once rather than after the cap.

**Why this before the `<http4-img>` component** (iss-pp8s2ym): it keeps the browser's preload scanner, which the component forfeits. The request still goes out as early as the browser wants; only the decision is deferred. It is a few lines against a new public API, and it needs no change to any page.

**What it cannot do**, and what still justifies the component: the first visit, where no worker controls the page at all ([[fnd-hnymjv8]]).

The fallback reason now names the timeout that expired ("not ready after 400 ms"), so a slow bootstrap can be told apart from a session that never came — the distinction that cost hours of guessing on the live deployment.

**Unmeasured.** These three numbers are reasoned, not tuned. 400 ms could still be too much first-paint risk on a page whose CSS would otherwise have arrived instantly, and 6 s could be too long where WebTransport is silently blocked and every image eats the full cap. Measure under netem (not DevTools throttling — [[fnd-sgw2sbh]]) on a fast path and a slow one, first visit and repeat, reporting share of bytes over HTTP4 *and* LCP, before treating any of them as settled.

payload.title: HTTP4 halves LCP on a real network path (120.0 ms vs 239.0 ms) while finishing bulk 25% later — the designed trade, measured
payload.body:
Two DevTools traces of the live demo, captured back to back on 2026-09-23 10:17–10:18, no throttling, over the LAN path to the VM, with the bootstrap changes in place (inline config, relative `/wt`, adaptive worker hold). Same page, same 6.3 MiB.

| metric | HTTP/2 (`?http4=off`) | HTTP4 | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| DOMContentLoaded | 203.7 ms | 81.1 ms | **−60.2%** |
| FCP / LCP | 238.9 ms | **120.0 ms** | **−49.8%** |
| loadEventEnd | 272.8 ms | 341.8 ms | +25.3% |
| share of bytes over HTTP4 | 0.0% | **98.9%** | |

**This is the shape the protocol was designed to produce.** First paint arrives in half the time because the stylesheet, script and small assets are delivered first; the page finishes 25% later because the largest images are deliberately deferred behind them. The user has already noted that deferring bulk to serve latency-sensitive work is a feature, not a regression — this is the first measurement on real infrastructure where that trade is visible and favourable.

SRPT ordering is again exact in the HTTP4 run — twelve images completing in strictly ascending size order (150 KiB at 95.0 ms → 1053 KiB at 341.1 ms) — while HTTP/2's order is unrelated to size (893 KiB finishes at 234.9 ms, before the 150 KiB one at 243.9 ms).

**A correction to my own method, which invalidated an earlier reading.** I had been classifying a resource as HTTP4-delivered when it showed no network bytes. That is wrong: a cache hit looks identical, and on this pair it produced the absurd result that the `?http4=off` run was "98.9% over HTTP4". The sound discriminator is in `ResourceReceiveResponse`: a worker-served HTTP4 response is *synthesised* from transferred bytes and carries `fromServiceWorker: true`, `protocol: "http/1.1"`, `encodedDataLength: 0`, whereas a passthrough carries the real `protocol` (`h2` here) and real bytes. Re-checked with that rule, the earlier LAN and 3G conclusions still stand — 98.9% and 0.0% respectively — but they stood by luck rather than by method.

**Caveats.** One run per stack, no repeats; [[fnd-q7mn3zg]] showed a controlled baseline can vary up to 3× between runs, so treat the magnitudes as indicative. The absolute numbers are also ~5× faster than the earlier LAN session ([[fnd-jek9y6q]]: LCP 1127.7/1305.9 ms), so conditions differed between sessions and **only the within-session A/B is comparable**. What changed in the code between them — the inline config removing a round trip, and the adaptive hold ([[dec-s6ff87p]]) keeping images on HTTP4 — is consistent with the improvement but not isolated by this measurement.

payload.body:
Four DevTools traces of the live demo on 2026-09-23 10:34–10:40, over the LAN to the VM with `netem` impairment applied on the VM's interface (shaping TCP and UDP alike, outside the browser — not DevTools throttling). Two runs per stack, alternating. Effective throughput 0.26–0.39 MiB/s, so the path was genuinely constrained. Same page, 6.19 MiB, HTTP4 share 98.9% in both HTTP4 runs and 0.0% in both `?http4=off` runs.

| | h2 (five / four) | HTTP4 (three / six) |
|---|---|---|
| font (lora woff2) | 12721 / 10639 ms | **1124 / 1158 ms** |
| 1st image | 2286 / 1846 ms | 1278 / 1098 ms |
| 3rd image | 7700 / 4820 ms | 2651 / 2838 ms |
| median image | 12948 / 10960 ms | **6413 / 8237 ms** |
| 9th image | 15564 / 12794 ms | 13039 / 13049 ms |
| last image | 20115 / 15884 ms | 21803 / 23415 ms |
| loadEventEnd | 20116 / 15885 ms | 21803 / 23416 ms |
| throughput | 0.31 / 0.39 MiB/s | 0.28 / 0.26 MiB/s |

**The font is the headline, and no standard metric shows it.** Over HTTP/2 the typeface arrives around 11 seconds, so the page reads in fallback text for that entire time; over HTTP4 it lands at ~1.1 s. A ~10× difference in the thing a reader notices most. The operator reported seeing the difference visually before any trace was analysed.

Images tell the same story with a clear crossover: HTTP4 is roughly 2× sooner for the first three, ~35% sooner at the median, level by the 9th, and behind on the last. That is SRPT doing exactly what it claims, and the deferred tail is the intended trade.

**The throughput gap is not part of that trade and is a real cost.** HTTP4 moved 0.26–0.28 MiB/s where HTTP/2 moved 0.31–0.39 — roughly 20% less on the same shaped path. It is consistent with [[fnd-jek9y6q]] and iss-pjpnk4q, where HTTP4 sustained ~16 MiB/s against HTTP/2's ~75 on an unconstrained LAN. Being slower per byte *and* deliberately reordering means part of the front-loading win is being paid for twice.

**LCP is not a useful metric for this page.** It came out 631.7 / 862.4 ms for HTTP4 against 655.1 / 372.1 ms for h2 — mixed and inconsistent between runs, because LCP tracks whichever element happens to be the largest painted on an image grid. The percentile table above describes the delivered experience far better, and future comparisons should report per-resource percentiles rather than leaning on LCP.

**Caveats.** Two runs per stack. The two h2 runs differed by 26% in throughput (0.31 vs 0.39 MiB/s), so conditions were not perfectly held, and every magnitude here should be read as approximate. The exact netem parameters were set on the VM and are not recorded in the traces; future runs should note them alongside the files.

On a delay-only path, throughput is set by how well each stack's congestion control fills the bandwidth-delay product — so this compares quic-go's behaviour against the kernel's TCP, on top of any HTTP4-specific limit. It is consistent with [[fnd-jek9y6q]] and iss-pjpnk4q (~16 MiB/s vs ~75 MiB/s on an unconstrained LAN), but this run cannot separate "HTTP4's grant mechanism under-fills the pipe" from "quic-go's congestion control is less aggressive than TCP's here".

**LCP is not a useful metric for this page.** It came out 631.7 / 862.4 ms for HTTP4 against 655.1 / 372.1 ms for h2 — mixed and inconsistent between runs, because LCP tracks whichever element happens to be the largest painted on an image grid. The percentile table above describes the delivered experience far better, and future comparisons should report per-resource percentiles rather than leaning on LCP.

**Caveats.** Two runs per stack. The two h2 runs differed by 26% in throughput (0.31 vs 0.39 MiB/s), so conditions were not held steady, and every magnitude here should be read as approximate. Record the `tc qdisc show` line alongside future traces, and separate latency from bandwidth by running delay-only and cap-only conditions rather than whatever combination happened to be active.

payload.title: Against HTTP/3, most of HTTP4's apparent advantage disappears: the font win was HTTP/2's head-of-line blocking, not HTTP4's scheduling
payload.body:
First comparison against a real HTTP/3 baseline, using the new `-alt-svc` flag so the `?http4=off` arm is upgraded to HTTP/3 rather than HTTP/2. Two traces, 2026-09-23 11:09 and 11:10, same VM, same netem impairment, same page (6.19 MiB). Verified from the traces: in the baseline all 13 images and the font carry `protocol: "h3"`, and the HTTP4 arm carries the synthesised `http/1.1` marker with a 98.9% share.

| | HTTP4 (seven) | HTTP/3 (eight) | winner |
|---|---|---|---|
| DOMContentLoaded | 619.0 ms | 436.8 ms | HTTP/3 |
| LCP | 611.9 ms | 470.7 ms | HTTP/3 |
| font | 946.4 ms | 698.6 ms | HTTP/3 |
| 1st image | 1026 ms | 3456 ms | **HTTP4** |
| median image | 7835 ms | 11188 ms | **HTTP4** |
| last image | 21526 ms | 16640 ms | HTTP/3 |
| loadEventEnd | 21526.5 ms | 16640.7 ms | HTTP/3 |
| throughput | 0.29 MiB/s | 0.37 MiB/s | HTTP/3 |

**The headline of [[fnd-f9mjfas]] does not survive.** That finding reported the font arriving ~10× sooner over HTTP4 (≈1.1 s against ≈11 s) and treated it as the clearest evidence for receiver-driven scheduling. Against HTTP/3 the same font arrives in **698.6 ms — sooner than HTTP4's 946.4 ms**. So the ~11 s figure was not a property of HTTP/2's *scheduling* at all; it was TCP head-of-line blocking on a high-latency path, which HTTP/3 does not have. **We were measuring HTTP/2's weakness and crediting it to HTTP4.**

**What does survive, and it is real:** HTTP4 delivers the first image at 1026 ms against HTTP/3's 3456 ms, and the median image at 7835 ms against 11188 ms — roughly 3× and 30% sooner respectively. That is SRPT genuinely ordering bulk better than HTTP/3's own prioritisation, on a transport with the same congestion control and no head-of-line blocking on either side. It is a narrower claim than "10× on the font", but it is a claim about scheduling rather than about the baseline's defects, which makes it worth more.

**What HTTP4 loses on:** first paint (LCP 611.9 vs 470.7), DOMContentLoaded, the tail (21.5 s vs 16.6 s), and throughput (0.29 vs 0.37 MiB/s, ~22% less). The throughput gap is consistent across every path measured so far ([[fnd-jek9y6q]], [[fnd-f9mjfas]], iss-pjpnk4q) and is now the single most consequential open problem: HTTP4 reorders bytes better while moving fewer of them, and the second cost partly cancels the first.

**Implication for the project's claims.** Every comparison before this one used HTTP/2 as the baseline, and HTTP/2 is not what HTTP4 would displace — a site deploying HTTP4 over WebTransport could deploy HTTP/3 instead for far less effort. HTTP/3 is the honest competitor, and results against it should be treated as the ones that matter. [[fnd-9s48fb0]] (LCP 120 vs 239 ms) and [[fnd-f9mjfas]] should both be read as HTTP/2 comparisons and re-run against HTTP/3 before being cited.

**Caveats.** One run per stack. Throughput differed by 28% between the arms (0.29 vs 0.37 MiB/s), which is the same order as the run-to-run variation seen elsewhere, so the smaller differences here (LCP, DCL, font) are within the noise this measurement can resolve. The image ordering results are large enough to be outside it. The exact netem parameters were again not captured.

payload.title: The tail is throughput-bound, not schedule-bound: no SRPT tuning can improve it, because last-byte time is total ÷ throughput
payload.body:
Asked whether the scheduler could give larger responses a bigger share so the tail catches up. The arithmetic on the HTTP/3 comparison ([[fnd-1yy7zyq]]) says no, decisively.

In both arms the last byte lands at exactly total bytes ÷ achieved throughput:

| | last byte | total ÷ throughput | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP4 | 21.53 s | 6.19 MiB ÷ 0.29 MiB/s = 21.34 s | 1.008 |
| HTTP/3 | 16.64 s | 6.19 MiB ÷ 0.37 MiB/s = 16.73 s | 0.995 |

Both links are saturated for the whole transfer. **When the link is saturated, scheduling determines only which resource finishes when — never when the last one does.** Total work is conserved: every byte given to a large response is taken from a small one. So a weighted policy, a reserved share for the longest transfer, a per-transfer floor, or k-way SRPT would all delay the early resources without the page finishing any sooner. It would move HTTP4's delivery profile toward HTTP/3's while giving up the first-image and median-image advantages that are the only things HTTP4 is currently winning.

**The whole 21.5 s vs 16.6 s tail gap is the ~22% throughput deficit** (0.29 vs 0.37 MiB/s), which is a separate problem with a separate cause (iss-pjpnk4q). Close that and the tail closes with it, at no cost to the ordering win.

This redirects effort: **stop looking at the scheduler for tail performance.** The scheduler is doing its job. Scheduling work is worth doing for other reasons — application-controlled priorities (G10, iss-j9tm9w8) change *which* resource is favoured, and starvation prevention (G6) protects a transfer that would otherwise never complete — but neither is a lever on total completion time under saturation.

Caveat: this holds while the link is saturated, which both arms were. On an unsaturated path (a fast LAN, or a page smaller than the bandwidth-delay product) the last-byte time is not throughput-bound and the reasoning does not apply — though there the tail is short enough not to matter.

sources.note: derived from Trace-20260923T110923-seven / 111049-eight; last-byte = total/throughput within 1% in both arms

patch.body:
From [[fnd-jek9y6q]] (LAN: HTTP4 ~16 MiB/s against HTTP/2's ~75), [[fnd-f9mjfas]] (high-latency vs HTTP/2: 0.26–0.28 against 0.31–0.39 MiB/s) and [[fnd-1yy7zyq]] (high-latency vs **HTTP/3**: 0.29 against 0.37 MiB/s, ~22% less). The deficit appears on every path measured so far, and [[fnd-m1r3sdp]] shows it is the *only* thing setting the tail: under saturation the last byte lands at total ÷ throughput, so closing this gap closes the tail for free and no scheduler change can.

**Corrected 2026-09-23 after reading the code. The two hypotheses this issue led with are both wrong:**

- *"Grants are issued on a timer, so the rate is budget ÷ tick interval."* **False.** `transport.ts:483` calls `pumpGrants()` after every decoded datagram, so grants are issued on arrival, not on a schedule. The `setInterval` at `transport.ts:618` is the recovery/stall tick, not the grant path.
- *"quic-go's congestion control is less aggressive than the kernel's TCP."* **Not applicable to the HTTP/3 comparison.** With `-alt-svc` the h3 baseline is served by the *same quic-go server on the same UDP port*, so both arms share one congestion controller. Whatever costs the 22% is in the HTTP4 datagram path itself, not in the transport underneath it.

The budget also does not obviously bind. It is `clamp(2 × maxRate × minRtt, 128 KiB, 16 MiB)`; at the impaired RTT a 128 KiB floor permits far more than the 0.29 MiB/s observed, so the floor is not the ceiling here. (On a sub-millisecond LAN the arithmetic is different and the floor may well bind — that case is still open.)

**What is actually left, in order of how cheaply it can be tested:**

1. **Repair overhead.** QUIC does not retransmit datagrams, so HTTP4 does its own loss repair, while the h3 arm gets QUIC's retransmission for free. Every resent or duplicated byte is throughput spent twice. **Measure first:** `/metrics.json` gives `data_bytes` and `resent_bytes` server-side, and `window.__http4.stats()` gives `duplicateBytesIn`, `resendsSent`, `recoveries`, `reqRetransmits`. If `resent_bytes / data_bytes` is near 22%, the answer is here and nothing else needs investigating.
2. **Grant-loop latency.** The sender may send only up to the granted ceiling, and a GRANT takes a round trip to arrive. If the budget is not kept at least a BDP ahead of the frontier, the sender idles waiting for permission — a cost the h3 arm does not pay, since QUIC's flow-control window is managed in the transport. Check the frontier-to-ceiling gap over time, and how often the sender has nothing granted to send.
3. **Datagram-path efficiency.** Per-datagram overhead in the browser (one JS callback per 1183-byte payload) and on the server (`SendDatagram` per packet) against QUIC's stream framing. Measure datagrams/second and compare against the h3 arm's packet rate.
4. **The 128 KiB budget floor on fast paths**, which remains the leading candidate for the LAN case specifically ([[fnd-jek9y6q]]), where 16 MiB/s ÷ 128 KiB ≈ 128 grant cycles/s.

**Why this is now the highest-value open problem.** HTTP4 currently beats HTTP/3 on first image (~3×) and median image (~30%) and loses on first paint, DOMContentLoaded, the tail and throughput. The tail is throughput-bound, so this one gap accounts for that loss entirely, and partly cancels the ordering win it is paying for.

Acceptance: the dominant cause is identified with evidence and either fixed or recorded as an accepted limit with the reason. Re-run the HTTP/3 comparison afterwards and report throughput alongside the per-resource percentiles.

patch.title: Close the ~22% throughput deficit in the HTTP4 datagram path (it sets the tail, and no scheduling change can)

payload.title: The throughput deficit is not HTTP4's protocol logic: repair costs 1.1% and the sender is blocked in SendDatagram 99.8% of the time
payload.body:
Server metrics from a single clean page load over HTTP4 on the live demo (netem-impaired path, 2026-09-23), read from `/metrics.json` on the VM's loopback. This was taken to decide between the four hypotheses in iss-pjpnk4q, and it eliminates the top two.

```
data_bytes          6,493,199      resent_bytes       72,897
data_packets            5,528      send_blocked        1,944
send_blocked_micros 21,447,235     ungranted_bytes_sent    0
seq_resends                57      seq_resend_misses       0
```

Derived, against ~21.5 s wall and 6,420,302 eligible bytes:

| | |
|---|---|
| repair overhead (`resent/data`) | **1.12%** |
| payload delivered | 6,420,302 B — exactly the eligible bytes |
| sends that blocked | 1944 / 5528 = 35.2% |
| **time blocked in SendDatagram** | **21.45 s of ~21.5 s = 99.8% of wall** |
| average block | 11.0 ms |
| wire interval | 3.89 ms per datagram |

**Hypothesis 1 (repair overhead) is dead.** 1.12% cannot explain a 22% deficit. HTTP4's own loss repair is cheap on this path, and `seq_resend_misses: 0` shows the sequence table never ran out either.

**Hypothesis 2 (grant-loop latency) is dead.** The sender was blocked inside `SendDatagram` for 99.8% of the transfer. A sender starved of grants would be *idle*, waiting for permission to send; this one always had work and was permanently backpressured by quic-go. So the receiver's grant loop is keeping comfortably ahead of the wire, and the round trip a GRANT costs is not showing up as sender idle time. (Consistent with the code: `transport.ts:483` pumps grants after every decoded datagram, not on a timer.)

**What that leaves.** HTTP4's protocol logic is not the bottleneck at all — it offers bytes faster than quic-go will accept them, continuously. Since the HTTP/3 baseline runs on the *same quic-go server and the same UDP port* ([[fnd-1yy7zyq]]), the difference must be in how quic-go treats **datagrams versus streams**: datagrams go through a 32-deep send queue with `SendDatagram` blocking when full, while stream data is buffered and drained opportunistically by the packetiser. That is a structural difference in how completely each can fill the congestion window, and it sits below anything this project controls.

**Consequences if that holds.** The deficit would not be fixable in HTTP4's scheduler, budget or repair logic. The available moves would be: raise or bypass quic-go's datagram queue depth (it is an unexported constant, `quicSendQueue = 32` is mirrored in `pacer.go`), send some or all body bytes over QUIC streams rather than datagrams, or accept the cost and say so. Each is a significant design question, not a tuning knob.

**Also confirmed in passing:** `ungranted_bytes_sent: 0` — G2 holds under real load on a real network, not just in the test harness.

**Caveat.** One load, one path. The 11.0 ms average block against a 3.89 ms wire interval suggests bursty delivery (netem batching) rather than a steady drain, so the blocking figure should be re-checked on a clean path before the quic-go conclusion is treated as established. The decisive next measurement is the same counters from an *unimpaired* run, plus the equivalent packet rate from the h3 arm.

patch.body:
Server metrics from clean page loads over HTTP4 on the live demo (2026-09-23), read from `/metrics.json` on the VM's loopback, taken to decide between the four hypotheses in iss-pjpnk4q. Two runs: one with netem impairment, one with netem cleared.

| | impaired | clean |
|---|---|---|
| data_bytes | 6,493,199 | 6,420,302 |
| resent_bytes | 72,897 (**1.12%**) | **0** |
| data_packets | 5,528 | 5,478 |
| bytes / packet | 1175 | 1172 |
| sends blocked | 1944 / 5528 = 35.2% | **6 / 5478 = 0.1%** |
| time blocked in SendDatagram | 21.45 s ≈ **99.8% of wall** | **11.3 ms** |
| seq_resend_misses | 0 | 0 |
| ungranted_bytes_sent | 0 | 0 |

**Hypothesis 1 (repair overhead) is dead.** 1.12% impaired, and exactly 0 on a clean path, cannot explain a 22% deficit.

**Hypothesis 2 (grant-loop latency) is dead.** On the impaired path the sender was blocked in `SendDatagram` for 99.8% of the transfer. A sender starved of grants would be *idle* waiting for permission; this one always had granted work and was backpressured by the wire.

**CORRECTED, same day: the clean run refutes the conclusion the impaired run alone suggested.** From the impaired numbers I concluded the deficit lived in quic-go's datagram path — a 32-deep send queue limiting how full the congestion window could be kept. The clean run shows the sender blocked **6 times in 5478 sends**. quic-go accepts datagrams as fast as HTTP4 offers them whenever the wire allows. The 99.8% blocking under netem simply means *the wire was slow*, which is the correct and expected behaviour of a sender pushing into a constrained path — not evidence of a queue limit. **quic-go's datagram queue is not the bottleneck, and my reading of the first dump was wrong.**

**What the clean run implies instead.** On a fast path HTTP4 reached ~16 MiB/s against HTTP/2's ~75 ([[fnd-jek9y6q]]) while *never* being blocked by quic-go. So on an unconstrained path the limit is **above** `SendDatagram` — in HTTP4 itself or in the browser. At 1172 bytes per datagram, 16 MiB/s is ~14,000 datagrams per second, each one a separate JavaScript callback on the receiving side; the LAN traces showed the main thread 60–92% busy through the transfer. **Hypothesis 3 (per-datagram overhead) is now the leading explanation for the fast-path ceiling**, and it is testable: measure datagrams/second at saturation and the per-datagram cost in the client.

**And the impaired-path "22% deficit" may not be real.** 0.29 against 0.37 MiB/s is a 28% spread, but two *same-stack* HTTP/2 runs differed by 26% (0.31 vs 0.39, [[fnd-f9mjfas]]), and the netem parameters were never captured. A difference of that size is inside the run-to-run variation this setup has repeatedly shown. It should not be treated as an established deficit until measured with held conditions and repeats.

**Confirmed in passing, and worth keeping:** `ungranted_bytes_sent: 0` on both runs — G2 holds under real load on a real network, not only in the harness. And on the clean run `data_bytes` equals the eligible bytes *exactly*, with `resent_bytes`, `seq_resends` and `seq_resend_misses` all zero: a perfect transfer with no waste.

patch.title: Repair and grant latency both ruled out; on a clean path the sender is never blocked, so the fast-path ceiling is above SendDatagram

payload.title: The fast-path ceiling is the grant budget sized on network RTT, while the latency that matters is per-datagram processing — 30× larger
payload.body:
Clean-LAN trace of the live demo (2026-09-23, netem cleared, cache disabled, HTTP4 share 98.9%): **6.19 MiB in 470.4 ms = 13.16 MiB/s**, matching the ~16 MiB/s seen earlier ([[fnd-jek9y6q]]). Combined with the server's `/metrics.json` from the same configuration ([[fnd-x833e37]]: 5478 datagrams, sender blocked 6 times), this identifies the ceiling.

**The arithmetic.** Throughput is bounded by in-flight bytes ÷ the latency to turn them over:

| | |
|---|---|
| measured throughput | 13.80 MB/s |
| grant budget | 131,072 B (the floor) |
| **implied in-flight latency** | **9.50 ms** |
| LAN network RTT | ~0.3 ms |
| **not the wire** | **~9.2 ms** |

Main thread over the same window: 6764 tasks, 187.1 ms busy = **39.8%** of the 470 ms — 1.23 tasks and 34.2 µs per datagram, at 11,655 datagrams/s. Nothing is saturated: the sender is not blocked by quic-go, the receiver has ~2.5× CPU headroom, and the wire is idle most of the time.

**The mechanism.** The budget is `clamp(2 × maxRate × minRtt, 128 KiB, 16 MiB)`. On this path that is `2 × 13.8 MB/s × 0.3 ms ≈ 8 KB`, far below the floor, so **the budget sits at 128 KiB permanently** and throughput is fixed at 128 KiB ÷ 9.5 ms.

`minRtt` is measured from GRANT probes — a *network* round trip. But the latency that decides how much must be in flight is the **delivery** latency, which here is 30× larger because it includes the client's per-datagram processing: Chrome delivers each datagram as its own task, and 111 datagrams (one budget's worth) take ~9.5 ms of wall time to arrive and be handled. Sizing the pipe on network RTT under-provisions it exactly when processing latency dominates, which is the fast-path case. The comment in `budget.ts` explains why `minRtt` is preferred over `srtt` — queueing inflates `srtt` when the pipe is full — and that reasoning is sound for a congested path, but it also excludes the one component that dominates on an uncongested one.

**Falsifiable prediction.** Raising the floor should raise LAN throughput close to proportionally until the main thread saturates, i.e. up to roughly 2.5× (~33 MiB/s) before per-datagram CPU becomes the binding constraint. If raising the floor does *not* raise throughput, this explanation is wrong and the limit is elsewhere.

**Two candidate fixes, to be decided on measurement:**
1. **Raise the floor** — one constant, immediate, but arbitrary: it trades memory and browser datagram-queue depth for throughput on every path, and a floor chosen for a LAN may be wrong for a phone.
2. **Size the budget on measured delivery latency rather than network RTT** — the principled fix. The receiver can measure the wall time from granting to receiving those bytes, which captures processing and wire alike, and needs no new wire format. More work, and it must not reintroduce the `srtt` inflation problem the current design deliberately avoids.

**Caveat.** One trace, one machine, one page. The 9.5 ms figure is derived, not directly observed; the direct check is the client's `stats.budget`, `stats.minRttMs` and the GRANT interval, which this trace does not carry. Confirm those before acting.

payload.title: The UDP receive buffer was the fast-path bottleneck; fixing it cut loss 5× and moved the limit to grant cadence
payload.body:
Two `/metrics.json` reads from clean-LAN page loads on the live demo (`tc qdisc show` confirmed `fq_codel`, no netem), before and after applying `net.core.rmem_max` / `wmem_max` = 7,500,000 on the VM. Same page, ~6.42 MB, ~5,470 datagrams each.

| | before the sysctl | after |
|---|---|---|
| `send_micros` (total time handing datagrams to quic-go) | 781.7 ms | **50.7 ms** |
| `send_blocked_micros` (waits ≥ 1 ms) | 669.2 ms in 221 calls | 9.8 ms in 6 calls |
| `send_ungranted_micros` (starved of grants) | 2.6 ms in 6 waits | **196.0 ms in 100 waits** |
| `resent_bytes` | 5,895 (**0.092%**) | 1,179 (0.018%) |

**The chain.** An undersized UDP receive buffer dropped ~1 datagram in 1,100 on a *switched LAN*, where there should be none. quic-go reads that as congestion, holds the window small, and backpressures the sender — 669 ms of it. Mathis puts loss-driven throughput at 5.7 MB/s for that loss rate and a 6.9 ms RTT; CUBIC beats Reno, and the observed ~13.8 MB/s is the right order. Raising the buffer cut loss 5× and `send_micros` by 15×.

**The bottleneck then moved to somewhere we control.** With the wire no longer the constraint, the sender now spends 196 ms starved of grants — 100 waits averaging 1.96 ms — while handing off datagrams takes only 50.7 ms in total. Every earlier suspect pointed outside this project (congestion control, kernel buffers, quic-go's internals); **grant cadence is `scheduler.ts` and `budget.ts`**, and it is the first limit that is ours to fix. That is the subject of iss-pjpnk4q from here.

**Why the sender starves at all is not yet explained.** The client's budget read 834 KB at the end of a load, and a sender holding 834 KB of granted-but-unsent bytes would run ~60 ms before exhausting them, not ~2 ms. Either the budget spends most of a short transfer still ramping from its 128 KiB floor (it doubles per round trip, so a ~300 ms load may never reach steady state), or the scheduler is not deploying what it has. `grantsSent` against the 100 starved waits separates those and has not been captured yet.

**Operational consequence, and a correction to advice I gave earlier the same day.** Told about quic-go's "failed to sufficiently increase receive buffer size" warning, I said it costs dropped datagrams under load but was not the cause of the fallback being investigated. That was true and beside the point: **the buffer was the single largest performance factor found so far**, worth a 15× reduction in sender blocking. It is not an advisory warning to defer. It belongs in the deployment checklist as a required step, and in the deploy doctor (iss-m84wtxx), with the container caveat that `net.core.rmem_max` is not network-namespaced and must be set on the host.

Two back-to-back traces of the live demo on 2026-09-23 14:39–14:40: clean LAN (no netem), UDP receive buffer already raised ([[fnd-649tzs7]]), HTTP/3 baseline via `-alt-svc`. Verified from the traces: the baseline's 22 requests all carry `protocol: "h3"`; the HTTP4 arm carries the synthesised `http/1.1` marker at a 98.9% share. Same page, 6.19 MiB.

| metric | HTTP4 | HTTP/3 | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| DOMContentLoaded | 80.2 ms | 89.3 ms | **−10.2%** |
| LCP | 110.5 ms | 126.8 ms | **−12.9%** |
| font | 233.1 ms | 97.0 ms | +140.3% |
| 1st image | 229 ms | 97 ms | +136.1% |
| median image | 288 ms | 136 ms | +111.8% |
| loadEventEnd | 371.2 ms | 168.4 ms | +120.4% |
| **throughput** | **16.14 MiB/s** | **32.46 MiB/s** | **2.01×** |

**HTTP4 still paints first.** SRPT puts the stylesheet and script ahead of the bulk, so LCP lands 13% sooner and DOMContentLoaded 10% sooner. That is the mechanism doing what it claims, on a path where it has almost nothing to work with.

**Everything after first paint is ~2× behind, and the throughput ratio explains all of it.** [[fnd-m1r3sdp]] established that under saturation the last byte lands at total ÷ throughput; at exactly half the throughput, the tail is exactly twice as late. No separate explanation is needed for load, font or image timings — they are one number.

**This is the cleanest isolation of the deficit so far.** Same server, same quic-go build, same UDP port, same clean LAN, buffer fixed, runs one minute apart. Everything that previously confounded the comparison is gone. What remains is **QUIC streams versus QUIC datagrams**, and the ratio is 2.01×.

**It also bounds when SRPT's ordering is worth its cost.** On the impaired path ([[fnd-1yy7zyq]]) HTTP4 delivered the first image ~3× and the median ~30% sooner than HTTP/3. Here it loses both by >2×. Ordering pays when capacity is scarce enough to be worth allocating; on a fast path there is nothing to ration and only the handicap is left. Any claim about HTTP4's benefit therefore has to name the path it holds on.

**Open, and now the only thing that matters for this comparison:** why datagram delivery runs at half the rate of stream delivery through the same quic-go. iss-pjpnk4q has ruled out repair overhead (0% on a clean path), grant-loop starvation, the budget floor and the budget ramp (`grantsAtFloor` 11 of 341). Not yet ruled out: per-datagram cost on either side, and quic-go's own treatment of DATAGRAM frames against STREAM frames in packet assembly and pacing.

**Caveat.** One run per stack. Earlier same-stack pairs varied by up to 26%, so a 10–13% first-paint advantage is within the noise this setup has shown; the 2× figures are comfortably outside it.

payload.title: Reverse-proxy an HTTP/1.1 origin (Next.js and similar) so its responses can travel over HTTP4
payload.body:
Asked for 2026-09-23: put `http4d` in front of an existing app (e.g. Next.js on `localhost:3000`) and serve its responses over HTTP4, instead of serving a directory.

Two properties of the current design decide everything about how hard each part is.

**The protocol needs a complete, randomly-addressable body.** `sender.Asset.Body` is a `[]byte`; packet 0 carries `total_size` (u32); grants are byte offsets; a resend reads `asset[off:off+n]`. So a proxied response must be **fully buffered before the first byte is sent**. There is no chunked form.

**`Assets.Get(id string)` has no request context** — no headers, no cookies, no client identity. Assets are shared and addressed by ID alone. That is right for files and hazardous for anything personalized.

---

**Tier 1 — static, immutable assets. Modest work, most of the value.**

For Next.js this is `/_next/static/**`, images, fonts: content-hashed, immutable, identical for every user, and **the bulk of the bytes** — exactly the traffic SRPT is good at ordering.

- A `ProxyAssets` implementing `Assets`: on a miss, GET the origin, buffer, build an `Asset` from the upstream `Content-Type`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified` and `Cache-Control`.
- An allowlist of path prefixes that may be proxied this way, defaulting to nothing. Anything not matching keeps going over plain HTTP, which the Service Worker already handles.
- A bounded cache (size and entry count), keyed by path, revalidated by ETag. Without a bound, a large origin is a memory exhaustion vector.
- **Refuse to cache anything carrying `Set-Cookie`, `Authorization`, `Vary: Cookie` or `Cache-Control: private`.** Serving one user's response to another is the classic cache-poisoning bug, and the ID-keyed model makes it the default failure rather than an unlikely one.
- Flags: `-proxy http://localhost:3000`, `-proxy-paths /_next/static/,/images/`, `-proxy-cache-bytes`.

**Tier 2 — dynamic, per-user responses. Substantially harder.**

SSR pages and API routes are per-user at the same URL, so they cannot be shared by ID at all.
- Assets would have to be scoped per session, not per server, which the `Assets` interface does not express. Either widen it to take request context, or give each session a private asset namespace.
- Request headers (cookie, authorization) must reach the origin, and `Vary` must be honoured.
- Still fully buffered, so an SSR page's time-to-first-byte becomes its *whole* generation time.
- Given the buffering cost and the leakage risk, the honest default is: **do not proxy these over HTTP4**, leave them on plain HTTP, and use HTTP4 for the static bulk. Measure before assuming otherwise.

**Tier 3 — streaming responses. Needs a wire change.**

React streaming SSR and any `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` origin have no length up front, which `total_size` requires. Supporting them means a protocol change (a chunked or length-unknown transfer), and it would conflict with buffering entirely. Out of scope unless Tier 1 proves the rest worthwhile.

**Also out of scope, and fine:** non-GET/HEAD methods. `leaveToNetwork` already sends them to the network, so forms and mutations keep working over plain HTTP. A proxied site is inherently mixed-transport, and that is the design, not a gap.

---

**Acceptance for Tier 1:** `http4d serve -proxy http://localhost:3000 -proxy-paths /_next/static/` in front of a real Next.js build serves its static chunks over HTTP4 with G1 intact (bytes match the origin's) and G2 = 0; a response carrying `Set-Cookie` or `Cache-Control: private` is never served from the shared cache; the cache respects its byte bound under a load that exceeds it; and the app still works with JavaScript navigation and form posts. Report the share of page bytes that HTTP4 carried, since that is what decides whether Tier 2 is worth attempting.

payload.title: Small API fetches stuck behind static assets is an HTTP/2 problem: HTTP/3 fixes it as well as HTTP4 does (209 ms vs 230 ms)
payload.body:
Asked whether HTTP4 would help the common pattern where fast dynamic fetches are stuck behind bulk static assets. Measured directly from the demo's three small API responses (451 + 449 + 78 B) competing with twelve images (150 KiB – 1 MiB) on the same page.

| path | small API fetch | position vs bulk |
|---|---|---|
| impaired, **HTTP/2** | **9,999–10,291 ms** | finishes around the *median* image |
| impaired, **HTTP/3** | **209 ms** | ahead of every image (1st image 3456 ms) |
| impaired, **HTTP4** | **230 ms** | ahead of every image (1st image 1026 ms) |
| clean LAN, HTTP/3 | 44 ms | around the median image |
| clean LAN, HTTP4 | 145 ms | ahead of the median image |

**The pattern is real and severe on HTTP/2.** Ten seconds for a 451-byte response while images monopolise the connection. That is TCP head-of-line blocking: one connection, one byte stream, and a stall anywhere holds up everything behind it whatever the priority says.

**HTTP/3 already fixes it, and fixes it as well as HTTP4 does.** 209 ms against HTTP4's 230 ms on the identical impaired path, with HTTP/3 marginally ahead. Independent streams mean a small response is not trapped behind a large one, which is most of what SRPT buys here. On a clean LAN HTTP/3 is outright faster in absolute terms (44 ms vs 145 ms), because of the 2× throughput advantage in [[fnd-3dnh0wf]].

**This is the third time a dramatic HTTP4 result has turned out to measure HTTP/2's weakness rather than HTTP4's strength**, after the font ([[fnd-1yy7zyq]]) and the LCP comparison. The pattern is consistent enough to be a rule: *any HTTP4 advantage measured against HTTP/2 must be re-measured against HTTP/3 before it is believed.* HTTP/2 head-of-line blocking is the common cause, and it is fixed by a config change on infrastructure people already run.

**Consequence for the proxy work (iss-sz6a8zk).** If the motivation for proxying a Next.js app through HTTP4 is to stop static assets blocking dynamic fetches, **enabling HTTP/3 on the existing stack achieves the same thing** for a fraction of the effort and none of the buffering, cache-safety or per-user-response problems that issue enumerates. The proxy should be justified on something else, or not built.

**What HTTP4 still has that HTTP/3 does not**, and which this measurement does *not* test: ordering decided at the receiver, per byte, every round trip. HTTP/3's priorities are hints a server may ignore, set by browser heuristics. A page that needs a dynamic fetch to beat static assets *by policy* rather than by being smaller is iss-j9tm9w8 (the priority API), and that capability is genuinely absent from HTTP/3. SRPT alone does not beat HTTP/3 at the case measured here.

**Caveats.** One run per condition. The impaired runs' netem parameters were not captured. The HTTP/2 figures come from a different session than the HTTP/3 ones, so the 10 s vs 209 ms contrast spans conditions that were not held identical — but the gap is two orders of magnitude, far outside any variance seen.
